laws.title: 2021 Military Coup and SAC Rule
laws.subtitle: State Administration Council and Suspended Constitution
laws.fullDescription: On February 1, 2021, the Tatmadaw (Myanmar military) seized power in a coup, detaining State Counsellor Aung San Suu Kyi and President Win Myint, and suspending the 2008 constitution. The military established the State Administration Council (SAC) under Senior General Min Aung Hlaing, declared a state of emergency, and annulled the November 2020 election results (in which the NLD won a landslide). The coup triggered mass protests — the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) — and eventually armed resistance. Myanmar has been in a state of civil war since, with the SAC unable to consolidate control over large parts of the country.
laws.penalty: Participating in anti-coup protests: arrest, torture, imprisonment; CDM participation (refusing to work for junta): dismissal, arrest; displaying anti-coup symbols: imprisonment
exceptions: Foreign diplomats accredited to Myanmar retain some protection though movements are monitored
UN and ICRC staff have limited operational access under negotiated arrangements

quiz.q: What triggered the February 2021 Myanmar military coup?
options: A constitutional referendum failed
The military disputed the November 2020 election results claiming fraud — and seized power
The president voluntarily stepped down
A foreign power intervened
quiz.explanation: The Myanmar military justified its February 1, 2021 coup by claiming fraud in the November 2020 elections — in which the NLD won 83% of contested seats. International observers found no evidence of systematic fraud. The military's refusal to accept the election results triggered one of Asia's largest protest movements and eventually a civil war, as the military proved unable to legitimize or consolidate its rule.

laws.title: Political Prisoners and Mass Detention
laws.subtitle: 20,000+ Arrested Since Coup
laws.fullDescription: Since the February 2021 coup, the SAC has arrested over 20,000 people — including politicians, journalists, activists, doctors, teachers, and ordinary citizens who participated in protests or CDM. Aung San Suu Kyi was convicted on multiple charges by military tribunals and sentenced to 27 years imprisonment. Former President Win Myint also imprisoned. Many activists face charges under Section 505(a) of the Penal Code (incitement), the Telecommunications Law, and anti-terrorism legislation. Detention conditions are severe — torture documented in interrogation facilities. Deaths in custody regularly occur.
laws.penalty: Section 505(a) incitement: up to 3 years imprisonment; Telecommunications Law violations: up to 3 years; anti-terrorism charges: death penalty possible; peaceful protest: typically 1-3 years imprisonment
exceptions: Diplomatic pressure has occasionally secured release of detained foreigners
Elderly and seriously ill detainees occasionally released for health reasons under international pressure
laws.sourceLabel: Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma

quiz.q: How many years was Aung San Suu Kyi sentenced to by the military tribunal?
options: 5 years
12 years
27 years — on multiple charges including corruption and election fraud
Life imprisonment
quiz.explanation: Aung San Suu Kyi was convicted by military-controlled tribunals on multiple charges including corruption, violation of COVID-19 regulations, illegal import of walkie-talkies, and election fraud — all widely condemned internationally as politically motivated. Her total sentence reached 27 years, ensuring she would remain imprisoned for life given her age (mid-70s). The convictions are not recognized by democratic countries or human rights organizations.

laws.title: Civil Disobedience Movement
laws.subtitle: CDM — Mass Refusal to Serve the Junta
laws.fullDescription: The Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) began within days of the 2021 coup — with civil servants, medical workers, teachers, railway employees, and government workers refusing to work for the military government. At its peak, hundreds of thousands participated, crippling government functions. The SAC responded by firing CDM participants, blacklisting them from government employment, arresting leaders, and seizing their bank accounts. Many CDM participants fled to opposition-controlled areas or abroad. The CDM severely degraded junta governance capacity — hospitals stopped functioning, public services collapsed, contributing to the humanitarian crisis.
laws.penalty: CDM participation: dismissal from government employment, blacklisting, bank account seizure; CDM leadership: arrest warrants and imprisonment; continuing CDM activity: terrorism charges possible
exceptions: Some essential service workers negotiated informal accommodations — continuing critical functions while avoiding active junta cooperation
CDM participants in exile continue advocacy without Myanmar legal consequence

quiz.q: What was the primary tactic of Myanmar's Civil Disobedience Movement?
options: Armed resistance against military bases
Boycotting Chinese businesses
Mass refusal to work for the military government — civil servants, doctors, teachers stopping work
Street protests exclusively
quiz.explanation: The CDM's primary tactic was collective work refusal — civil servants, medical workers, teachers, and government employees refusing to continue working under the military government. This passive resistance strategy aimed to make the junta ungovernable by depriving it of the administrative capacity to function. Though the SAC responded with mass firings and arrests, CDM participation remained widespread and severely damaged junta governance capacity.

laws.title: People's Defence Force and Armed Resistance
laws.subtitle: PDF, NUG, and Civil War
laws.fullDescription: The Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH) — elected MPs who refused to recognize the coup — formed the National Unity Government (NUG) in April 2021. The NUG subsequently established the People's Defence Force (PDF) as its armed wing, calling on citizens to take up arms against the military. The PDF — mostly civilians with limited military training — operates alongside long-standing ethnic armed organizations (EAOs). Since 2021, Myanmar has been in escalating civil war. Operation 1027 (October 2023) saw a coordinated offensive by three Brotherhood Alliance EAOs that captured major territory, significantly weakening the SAC. As of 2024, the SAC controls less than 50% of Myanmar's territory.
laws.penalty: Membership in PDF: death penalty under SAC anti-terrorism law; supporting NUG: terrorism charges; hiding PDF members: imprisonment
exceptions: PDF and EAO members in areas under their control operate under their own governance systems
International humanitarian law applies to all parties — though enforcement is virtually impossible in active conflict zones

quiz.q: What was Operation 1027 in Myanmar?
options: A SAC military offensive to clear PDF from Sagaing Region
A coordinated Brotherhood Alliance offensive (October 2023) that captured significant territory from the SAC
A UN peacekeeping operation
A ceasefire agreement between SAC and EAOs
quiz.explanation: Operation 1027 (launched October 27, 2023) was a major coordinated offensive by the Three Brotherhood Alliance — comprising MNDAA (Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army), TNLA (Ta'ang National Liberation Army), and AA (Arakan Army) — that captured multiple towns, border crossings, and military bases from the SAC. The operation significantly shifted the conflict, demonstrating that the SAC military was far weaker than it appeared, and inspired other resistance forces to launch offensives across Myanmar.

laws.title: Rohingya Genocide and Persecution
laws.subtitle: 1 Million Refugees and ICJ Case
laws.fullDescription: The Rohingya — a Muslim minority in Rakhine State — have faced decades of persecution, statelessness under the 1982 Citizenship Law, and systematic violence. The 2017 military 'clearance operations' following ARSA attacks killed thousands, burned over 350 villages, and forced over 700,000 Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh (Cox's Bazar now hosts 1 million+ refugees — the world's largest refugee camp). The Gambia filed a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in 2019 under the Genocide Convention; provisional measures ordered Myanmar to protect the Rohingya. The ICC has opened an investigation. Rohingya remaining in Myanmar live in apartheid-like conditions in Rakhine State.
laws.penalty: Rohingya stateless: cannot travel, own property, access healthcare or education freely; ARSA membership: death penalty; returning Rohingya refugees: arrest and imprisonment
exceptions: Some Rohingya with National Verification Cards (NVC) have limited recognition — though NVC is not equivalent to citizenship
Humanitarian organizations (UNHCR, MSF) maintain limited access to Rohingya camps in Rakhine State

quiz.q: Which country filed a genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice?
options: Bangladesh
United States
The Gambia — under the Genocide Convention
United Kingdom
quiz.explanation: The Gambia — a small West African nation — filed a case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice in November 2019, alleging violations of the Genocide Convention in relation to the Rohingya. The Gambia acted on behalf of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The ICJ issued provisional measures in January 2020 ordering Myanmar to protect the Rohingya from genocide — measures Myanmar appealed but could not fully escape.

laws.title: Economic Collapse Post-Coup
laws.subtitle: Kyat Devaluation, Banking Crisis, and Poverty
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's economy has collapsed since the 2021 coup. The kyat (currency) lost 50%+ of its value. The banking sector has been severely disrupted — capital flight, withdrawal limits, and loss of confidence. Foreign investment fled. Tourism collapsed. GDP contracted sharply (10%+ in 2021-22). Major multinational companies departed — Total/TotalEnergies sold its gas assets (though revenue continued flowing to the SAC). Garment factories closed or relocated. The World Bank estimates poverty has nearly doubled — 40%+ of Burmese now below the poverty line (up from 24% pre-coup). Conflict disrupting agriculture threatens food security.
laws.penalty: Currency violations (informal exchange at market rates outside official channels): criminal prosecution; capital flight: asset confiscation; foreign currency transaction without authorization: imprisonment
exceptions: Humanitarian aid transactions exempt from some foreign exchange controls under OFAC and EU sanctions carve-outs
Informal currency markets (black market) function widely despite being technically illegal

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of Myanmar's population fell below the poverty line after the coup?
options: About 10% — minimal impact
Around 24% — unchanged from pre-coup
Approximately 40%+ — nearly double the pre-coup poverty rate
Over 60% fell into poverty
quiz.explanation: The World Bank estimates Myanmar's poverty rate nearly doubled following the 2021 coup — rising to approximately 40% of the population (up from 24% pre-coup). This dramatic increase reflects the combined impact of economic contraction, kyat devaluation, banking disruption, business closures, conflict displacement, and agricultural disruption. The economic consequences have been severe even for communities not directly affected by military violence.

laws.title: Torture and Extrajudicial Killings
laws.subtitle: Military Atrocities Against Civilians
laws.fullDescription: The SAC military has committed systematic torture and extrajudicial killings documented by OHCHR, HRW, Amnesty International, and independent investigators. Methods include: burning civilians alive in villages, aerial bombardment of civilian areas and schools, summary executions, sexual violence as a weapon of war, torture in detention (documented techniques include waterboarding, electric shocks, stress positions), and mass killings. The UN Special Advisory Commission found reasonable grounds to believe crimes against humanity and war crimes are being committed. The Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma (AAPPB) tracks deaths in custody — over 4,000 civilians killed in military operations.
laws.penalty: International law: SAC commanders face potential ICC charges for war crimes and crimes against humanity; SAC domestic law: military operations against 'terrorists' are legally authorized — no domestic accountability
exceptions: Some lower-level soldiers have faced SAC military courts for 'excessive' actions in isolated cases — generally token punishment
International criminal accountability potential through ICC, though Myanmar is not a Rome Statute member — ICC jurisdiction based on deportation through Bangladesh border

quiz.q: How does the ICC assert jurisdiction over Myanmar despite its not being a Rome Statute member?
options: Through a UNSC referral
Based on deportation of Rohingya through Bangladesh, which is an ICC member state
Myanmar secretly ratified the Rome Statute
Special universal jurisdiction rules apply
quiz.explanation: The ICC asserts jurisdiction over Myanmar crimes against the Rohingya based on a creative legal theory: because the deportation and persecution of Rohingya extended into Bangladesh — which IS an ICC member state — the ICC claims jurisdiction over crimes with effects on the territory of a member state. The Pre-Trial Chamber authorized this approach in 2019. This jurisdictional theory does not cover all Myanmar crimes, but allows the ICC to investigate the most serious Rohingya-related offenses.

laws.title: Healthcare Collapse
laws.subtitle: CDM Doctors, Hospital Attacks, and Medical Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's health system has collapsed since the 2021 coup. CDM participation by thousands of doctors, nurses, and health workers left public hospitals non-functional in many areas. The SAC arrested and killed healthcare workers who participated in CDM. Hospitals have been attacked and used as military bases. WHO and medical NGOs (MSF, IRC) face severe access restrictions. The military has specifically targeted underground medical workers providing care to resistance fighters and civilian conflict victims — treating them as military targets. COVID-19 vaccination campaigns were disrupted. Maternal mortality, preventable disease deaths, and trauma care failures have increased dramatically.
laws.penalty: Healthcare workers participating in CDM: arrest, imprisonment, firing; providing medical care to PDF members: potential terrorism charges and death penalty; underground clinics in conflict areas: military targeting
exceptions: ICRC and MSF maintain limited access under negotiated arrangements — though increasingly contested
Hospital facilities technically protected under Geneva Convention provisions — though Myanmar military has repeatedly violated this

quiz.q: What specific risk do medical workers face when treating injured PDF members?
options: Medical workers are fully protected under international law
Mild professional penalties for treating non-state actors
Potential terrorism charges and death penalty — SAC classifies PDF as terrorists making treating them an act of terrorism support
Only administrative warnings
quiz.explanation: Myanmar law under SAC classifies the PDF as a terrorist organization. Providing medical care to PDF members can therefore be charged as 'supporting terrorism' — a charge carrying the death penalty. This creates a profound humanitarian law violation: medical neutrality — the right to treat wounded regardless of political affiliation — is guaranteed under the Geneva Conventions but systematically violated by the SAC, which has arrested and killed healthcare workers for providing care.

laws.title: Jade Mining and Environmental Destruction
laws.subtitle: Hpakant and Opaque Extraction
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Hpakant (Kachin State) is the world's most important source of imperial jade — a gem of extraordinary value in Chinese culture. The jade mining industry, estimated at USD 31 billion annually (though most evades official accounting), is dominated by military-connected companies and Kachin Independence Army (KIA) tax revenue. Conditions are catastrophic: massive tailings mountains collapse on miners (hundreds killed annually), 100,000+ miners work in dangerous conditions, and the landscape is devastated by mechanized extraction. Corruption and opacity make the true scale unknown. Since the coup, military entities have tightened control over jade revenues.
laws.penalty: Mining without SAC permit: imprisonment and confiscation; local miners operating without licenses: fines and forced labor; environmental violations: effectively no enforcement
exceptions: Artisanal miners in de facto KIA-controlled areas operate under KIA taxation rather than SAC regulation
Traditional community jade collection (surface picking) in some areas tolerated without formal licensing

quiz.q: What makes Myanmar's Hpakant region globally unique?
options: It contains the world's largest diamond deposit
It is home to Myanmar's only uranium mine
It is the world's most important source of imperial jade — a gem of extraordinary value in Chinese culture
It produces 80% of the world's rubies
quiz.explanation: Hpakant in Kachin State is the world's most important source of imperial jade (jadeite) — the deep green stone that holds extraordinary cultural and monetary value in Chinese culture, where it is considered more precious than gold. Myanmar's jade industry was estimated at USD 31 billion annually in a major study, though most revenue evades official channels. The industry operates in brutal conditions, with massive tailings collapses killing hundreds of miners annually.

laws.title: Death Penalty and Executions
laws.subtitle: First Executions Since 1988
laws.fullDescription: In July 2022, Myanmar's SAC executed four political prisoners — the first executions in Myanmar since 1988. Those killed included prominent democracy activist Ko Jimmy (Kyaw Min Yu) and former NLD lawmaker Phyo Zeyar Thaw, both convicted by military tribunals on terrorism charges. The executions shocked the international community and prompted widespread condemnation. Myanmar's military courts have sentenced hundreds more to death for pro-democracy activities, PDF membership, and 'terrorism'. The SAC has conducted summary executions during military operations — with bodies abandoned in villages as a terror tactic.
laws.penalty: Terrorism charges (PDF membership, supporting resistance): death penalty; treason: death penalty; murder of SAC personnel: death penalty; many death sentences outstanding for political prisoners
exceptions: Presidential pardons occasionally announced for ordinary criminals — though not political prisoners
International pressure has prevented some high-profile executions — though did not save the four July 2022 victims
laws.sourceLabel: Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma

quiz.q: When were the last executions in Myanmar before the SAC resumed them in 2022?
options: 1988 — making the 2022 executions the first in 34 years
quiz.explanation: Myanmar had not conducted formal executions since 1988 — a 34-year de facto moratorium on the death penalty. The SAC's July 2022 executions of Ko Jimmy, Phyo Zeyar Thaw, and two others on terrorism charges ended this moratorium and signaled the junta's willingness to kill political opponents through legal processes in addition to extrajudicial killings. The executions provoked international condemnation and calls for increased sanctions.

laws.title: Ethnic Armed Organizations
laws.subtitle: Tatmadaw vs. EAOs — Decade-Long Conflicts
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has one of the world's longest-running civil conflicts — with multiple ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) fighting for autonomy or independence. Major EAOs include: KIA (Kachin Independence Army), RCSS/SSA (Restoration Council of Shan State), AA (Arakan Army), TNLA (Ta'ang National Liberation Army), MNDAA (Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army), KNU (Karen National Union, with armed KNLA wing), CNF (Chin National Front), and others. The 2015 National Ceasefire Agreement (NCA) had limited success. Since 2021, most EAOs have either maintained neutrality, allied with the NUG/PDF, or conducted their own offensives against the SAC.
laws.penalty: EAO membership: death penalty under SAC law; supporting EAO operations: terrorism charges; residing in EAO-controlled areas: legal risk when traveling to SAC territory
exceptions: NCA signatory EAOs (KNU, RCSS) had formal ceasefire status — though most have suspended this post-coup
EAO-controlled territories operate under EAO legal systems independent of SAC law

quiz.q: What was the significance of Operation 1027 for the ethnic armed movement?
options: It was a SAC offensive that defeated key EAOs
It demonstrated SAC military weakness and inspired resistance forces across Myanmar to launch their own offensives
It was a failed EAO attempt to capture Naypyidaw
It resulted in a UN-brokered ceasefire
quiz.explanation: Operation 1027's dramatic success — capturing significant territory, border crossings, and military bases from the SAC — demonstrated that the military was far weaker than its fearsome reputation suggested. This inspired resistance forces across Myanmar to launch their own offensives: in Sagaing, Magway, Kayah, Karen, and Chin regions. The domino effect transformed Myanmar's conflict from scattered resistance into a coordinated nationwide military challenge to SAC authority.

laws.title: Golden Triangle Drug Trade
laws.subtitle: Myanmar's Opium and Methamphetamine Dominance
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar is the world's largest opium producer (surpassing Afghanistan after the Taliban's 2022 ban) and a major methamphetamine producer. The Golden Triangle — the border area where Myanmar, Thailand, and Laos meet (particularly Shan State) — produces massive quantities of heroin and 'yaba' (methamphetamine tablets). The drug trade is intertwined with ethnic armed groups (UWSA — United Wa State Army — the largest non-state army in Southeast Asia, controls major drug territories) and military-connected businesses. UNODC estimates Myanmar opium cultivation surged 33% in 2022. The SAC has limited ability to enforce drug laws in EAO-controlled poppy areas.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking (large scale): death penalty; drug use: imprisonment; cultivation: destruction and imprisonment (in SAC-controlled areas); transportation: criminal prosecution
exceptions: UWSA and other EAO-controlled areas operate under their own drug policies — UWSA officially banned opium in 2005 but alternative crops have not fully replaced drug income
Subsistence opium use by elderly addicts in remote areas treated with some tolerance

quiz.q: What happened to Myanmar's position in global opium production after Afghanistan's 2022 ban?
options: Myanmar was unaffected — it was already the largest producer
Myanmar became the world's largest opium producer as Afghan production collapsed
Myanmar actually reduced its production
Myanmar and Afghanistan share equal production
quiz.explanation: After the Taliban imposed their sweeping opium ban in 2022 — dramatically reducing Afghan production — Myanmar became the world's largest opium producer. UNODC data showed Myanmar opium cultivation surged 33% in 2022, partly filling the supply vacuum. This shift has significant implications for global heroin markets, regional drug trafficking routes, and Myanmar's internal economy in Shan State where opium remains a primary livelihood for many communities.

laws.title: Internet Shutdowns and Digital Repression
laws.subtitle: SAC Telecommunications and Surveillance
laws.fullDescription: The SAC has conducted repeated internet shutdowns since the coup — particularly in conflict areas like Chin, Sagaing, and Kachin states. In the days following the coup, the internet was cut for days to prevent protest organization. Township-level internet outages have become routine — military cordon operations are preceded by communications blackouts to prevent civilian warnings and documentation of abuses. The SAC forced telecom operators (Telenor sold its Myanmar operation partly due to surveillance demands; MPT is military-controlled). VPN use has surged among Burmese but is increasingly targeted. Social media (particularly Facebook, which was the primary internet platform) was initially blocked.
laws.penalty: Anti-coup social media posts: imprisonment documented (Section 505a); VPN use: not formally banned but phone searches target it; sharing conflict documentation: terrorism charges possible
exceptions: Journalists accredited by SAC media minders have some protection — but independent reporting is essentially impossible
International organization secure communications generally tolerated for humanitarian coordination

quiz.q: Why did Telenor sell its Myanmar telecommunications operations after the coup?
options: Declining business due to economic contraction
Telenor was forced to implement military surveillance demands — installing equipment enabling mass surveillance — making continued operation ethically untenable
The SAC nationalized all foreign telecom companies
Telenor was offered an irresistible price
quiz.explanation: Telenor (Norwegian telecommunications company) sold its Myanmar operations in 2021 partly because the SAC demanded it install equipment enabling mass surveillance and provide user data to security services. This created an ethical dilemma: continue operating (and potentially facilitating human rights abuses through surveillance) or exit. Telenor chose to exit, selling to M1 Group for a significantly discounted price. The case highlighted the difficult choices faced by foreign companies in authoritarian markets.

laws.title: 2008 Constitution and Military Veto
laws.subtitle: 25% Parliamentary Seats for Military
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's 2008 constitution — drafted by the military and approved in a referendum marred by Cyclone Nargis (which killed 140,000 people) — was designed to ensure permanent military political power. Key provisions: 25% of parliamentary seats reserved for military appointees (a blocking minority for constitutional amendments requiring 75%+ support), president cannot have foreign family members (targeting Aung San Suu Kyi whose children hold British passports), and military retains control of defense, border, and home affairs ministries. The NLD won supermajorities in 2015 and 2020 but could never amend the constitution due to the military veto block. The 2021 coup suspended even this limited framework.
laws.penalty: Under SAC: advocating for the 2008 constitution (which the SAC itself suspended): ironic legal risk if seen as opposition; under previous NLD government: constitutional challenges could be brought through courts (now closed)
exceptions: NUG has issued its own constitutional framework (Federal Democracy Charter) — applying in liberated areas
The CRPH formally revoked the 2008 constitution — though without territorial control this has limited practical effect

quiz.q: How did the 2008 constitution guarantee military political power even under civilian government?
options: The military could veto any legislation
By reserving 25% of parliamentary seats for military appointees — a blocking minority preventing constitutional amendment
By requiring military approval for all cabinet appointments
By making the commander-in-chief the head of state
quiz.explanation: The 2008 constitution's most significant mechanism for permanent military power was reserving 25% of parliamentary seats for unelected military appointees. Since constitutional amendments require 75% of all parliamentary seats, and the military holds 25%, any constitutional change requires military approval — giving the Tatmadaw an absolute veto on its own reform. This design meant that even the NLD's landslide election victories could not lead to meaningful constitutional change.

laws.title: Sexual Violence as Weapon of War
laws.subtitle: SGBV Documented by UN Investigators
laws.fullDescription: UN investigators and human rights organizations have documented systematic sexual violence by Myanmar's military against civilians — particularly in Kachin, Shan, Rakhine, and Sagaing states. Methods include gang rape during village raids, rape and killing of civilians during 'clearance operations', rape of female political detainees, and sexual humiliation as interrogation. The UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) collects evidence for eventual prosecution. The Rohingya case documented mass rape during the 2017 operations. Since the coup, similar patterns have been documented against ethnic communities and coup protesters. Many survivors refuse to report for fear of retaliation.
laws.penalty: International law: sexual violence as a weapon of war constitutes a war crime and crime against humanity; SAC domestic law: no accountability — perpetrators protected; survivors reporting: risk of retaliation and 'honor' consequences
exceptions: UN IIMM collects evidence that may eventually be used in international prosecutions — though timeline is uncertain
Some survivor organizations document cases through secure reporting channels for eventual accountability
laws.sourceLabel: UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar

quiz.q: What is the IIMM and what role does it play regarding Myanmar?
options: International Investment Monitoring Mission — tracking economic sanctions
UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar — collecting evidence for future international prosecution
International Infantry Medical Mission — providing combat medical care
ASEAN-created ceasefire monitoring body
quiz.explanation: The UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) was established by the Human Rights Council to collect, consolidate, and preserve evidence of the most serious international crimes committed in Myanmar since 2011. Unlike earlier UN human rights bodies, the IIMM is explicitly designed as a prosecutorial support mechanism — building evidence files that could be used in future international prosecutions at the ICC, ICJ, or through universal jurisdiction in third countries.

laws.title: Cyclone Mocha and Climate Disasters
laws.subtitle: 2023 Cyclone and Compounding Humanitarian Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Cyclone Mocha struck Myanmar's Rakhine State and western regions in May 2023 — one of the most powerful tropical cyclones to hit the Bay of Bengal in decades. The storm hit areas already devastated by military violence and Rohingya persecution. Over 1 million people were affected; thousands killed. Rohingya in displacement camps near Sittwe bore the brunt. The SAC's disaster response was severely limited by governance failures, deliberate obstruction of international aid to Rakhine (citing conflict with the Arakan Army), and the general collapse of state capacity. Climate change is increasing cyclone intensity in the Bay of Bengal, making Myanmar — with its long Rakhine and Ayeyarwady coastal exposure — increasingly vulnerable.
laws.penalty: Under SAC: humanitarian organizations face access restrictions in conflict areas; independent disaster relief by non-authorized organizations: arrest risk; conflict journalism during disaster: military targeting
exceptions: UN OCHA emergency response operations receive some SAC authorization for acute disaster response
ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance (AHA Centre) has formal status in Myanmar — though limited access

quiz.q: Which community was especially vulnerable when Cyclone Mocha hit Rakhine State in 2023?
options: Wealthy Rakhine merchant communities
Buddhist monks in coastal monasteries
Rohingya living in displacement camps near Sittwe — already persecuted and now hit by one of the Bay of Bengal's most powerful cyclones
Foreign diplomatic community
quiz.explanation: Rohingya Muslims confined to displacement camps near Sittwe — the Rakhine State capital — were among the most vulnerable when Cyclone Mocha struck. Having been forcibly displaced from their villages since 2012, living in crowded camps with minimal durable infrastructure, the Rohingya had no resources to escape the storm. The SAC's obstruction of international aid access to Rakhine State (citing ongoing conflict with the Arakan Army) compounded the disaster's impact.

laws.title: Oil and Gas Revenue
laws.subtitle: Yadana Pipeline and Military Finances
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's offshore gas fields — particularly Yadana (discovered by Total/Unocal) and Yetagun — generate hundreds of millions of dollars annually in gas sales through the Yadana pipeline to Thailand. After the coup, TotalEnergies (France) and Chevron (USA) exited their Myanmar gas joint ventures, citing the junta's human rights abuses. However, gas continued flowing and revenue continues reaching MOGE (Myanmar Oil and Gas Enterprise) — a state company largely controlled by the military. Campaigns by human rights organizations to shut off Myanmar gas revenue have had partial success: European companies exited but Thai PTT and other regional buyers continue purchasing.
laws.penalty: Operating energy assets without SAC authorization: criminal prosecution; interfering with pipeline operations: terrorism charges; unauthorized oil/gas extraction: severe criminal penalties
exceptions: International energy companies exiting Myanmar face complex contractual unwinding — some face arbitration claims from the SAC
Force majeure claims allow some companies to suspend operations without full contractual termination

quiz.q: Why did TotalEnergies exit its Myanmar gas operations despite their high value?
options: The gas fields were depleted
Total was outbid by Chinese companies
Human rights obligations and investor pressure made operating under the military government untenable — Total cited complicity in funding the junta
The SAC nationalized all foreign energy assets
quiz.explanation: TotalEnergies (formerly Total) exited Myanmar in January 2022 — citing the 'deteriorating situation' and human rights obligations, noting that continued gas revenue flowing to the junta constituted complicity in funding military operations. The exit followed sustained campaigns by human rights organizations and investors arguing that gas revenue was the SAC's largest single revenue source. However, gas continued flowing after Total's exit, with PTTEP (Thailand) continuing as a key buyer.

laws.title: Child Soldiers and Forced Recruitment
laws.subtitle: Tatmadaw Conscription of Minors
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's military has a documented history of recruiting child soldiers — boys as young as 12-15 have been forcibly recruited by the Tatmadaw, often from train stations, bus stops, and public spaces. Since the coup and the military's manpower losses against PDF and EAO forces, forced adult conscription has been formalized (Military Service Law, February 2024 — mandatory service for men 18-35 and women 18-27). The UN Secretary-General's annual report on children in armed conflict has listed Myanmar's military as a grave violator for years. PDF and some EAOs have also been listed for child recruitment in some cases.
laws.penalty: Resisting SAC conscription: imprisonment and criminal prosecution; Military Service Law violations: up to 5 years imprisonment; child soldier recruitment: war crime under international law — no SAC accountability
exceptions: Ethnic minority youth in EAO-controlled areas may escape SAC conscription within their areas
University students had some formal exemptions — though enforcement has become more coercive

quiz.q: What law did the SAC announce in February 2024 regarding military service?
options: A voluntary military service incentive program
Mandatory military service for men 18-35 and women 18-27 — formalized conscription as SAC faces manpower shortages
A law extending professional military salaries
A child protection law banning under-18 military recruitment
quiz.explanation: The SAC announced mandatory military service under the Military Service Law in February 2024 — requiring men aged 18-35 and women aged 18-27 to serve in the military. The announcement triggered a mass exodus of young Myanmar citizens — many fleeing to neighboring Thailand, Malaysia, and India to avoid conscription. The law reflected the SAC's serious manpower shortage as PDF and EAO offensives killed or demoralized large numbers of military personnel.

laws.title: Deforestation and Land Concessions
laws.subtitle: Timber, Rubber, and Agricultural Land Grabs
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar experienced rapid deforestation — losing over 50% of forest cover from 1990-2020. Teak (Myanmar produces most of the world's natural teak) has been heavily logged. Chinese companies obtained massive rubber and banana plantation concessions in Kachin and Shan states — clearing large forest areas. The SAC has granted new concessions to military-connected companies. In conflict areas, deforestation is used as a military tactic — clearing cover for guerrilla fighters. WWF and international conservation organizations have largely withdrawn from Myanmar since the coup. Global demand for Myanmar teak continues in European furniture and boat-building markets (though EU has banned Myanmar teak imports).
laws.penalty: Illegal logging (without SAC permit): criminal prosecution; unauthorized land clearing: confiscation; teak export without permit: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Forest communities with customary land rights in EAO-controlled areas operate under EAO land governance
Emergency fuel wood collection by displacement communities: practically tolerated as survival necessity

quiz.q: What significant import ban did the EU implement regarding Myanmar?
options: Ban on all Myanmar agricultural imports
EU banned Myanmar jade imports
EU banned Myanmar teak imports — in response to the coup and human rights concerns
EU banned all Myanmar manufactured goods
quiz.explanation: The EU banned imports of Myanmar teak (and other specified timber products) as part of its sanctions response to the 2021 coup. Myanmar teak — valued for outdoor furniture, boat decking, and construction — is prized globally, and teak export revenue had provided the Myanmar government (and now the SAC) with significant income. The EU ban was designed to reduce revenue flowing to the junta, though other markets (India, China, Southeast Asia) continued purchasing Myanmar teak.

laws.title: Press Freedom and Journalist Persecution
laws.subtitle: Reporters Imprisoned, Killed, and Fled
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has become one of the world's most dangerous countries for journalists. After the coup, the SAC revoked the licenses of all independent media, issued arrest warrants for editors and reporters, and raided newsrooms. Journalists covering protests and military operations face terrorism charges. Multiple journalists have been killed covering the conflict. Several independent Myanmar media — Mizzima, Irrawaddy, Myanmar Now, DVB — relocated abroad (Thailand, India, Europe) and continue reporting in exile. The SAC uses the Electronic Transactions Law (Section 38), Telecommunications Law (Section 66d), and anti-terrorism legislation to criminalize journalism. Over 100 journalists remain imprisoned.
laws.penalty: Reporting without SAC media accreditation: imprisonment; sharing anti-coup content: 1-3 years under Section 505a; footage of military operations: terrorism charges; journalism for exile media: arrest warrants issued
exceptions: Foreign journalists with SAC accreditation can operate — under strict minder supervision and self-censorship pressure
Citizen journalists using encrypted reporting tools have some protection if identity is concealed

quiz.q: Where have major Myanmar independent media organizations relocated after the coup?
options: They continue operating inside Myanmar underground
They have shut down permanently
To exile — primarily Thailand, India, and Europe — continuing to report on Myanmar from abroad
To China, which granted them refuge
quiz.explanation: Major Myanmar independent media including The Irrawaddy, Mizzima, Myanmar Now, and DVB (Democratic Voice of Burma) relocated to exile — primarily Thailand, India, and Europe — after the SAC raided their offices, arrested staff, and revoked their licenses. Operating from exile, these outlets continue reporting on the conflict and human rights situation in Myanmar, providing crucial information to the international community and to Burmese people who access their content via VPN.

laws.title: Internal Displacement Crisis
laws.subtitle: 2 Million+ Internally Displaced Persons
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has over 2 million internally displaced persons (IDPs) — among Asia's largest displacement crises. Displacement has multiple causes: military operations burning villages (particularly in Sagaing, Magway, Chin, Kayah, and Karen states), fighting between SAC and resistance forces, ethnic conflict in Rakhine and Shan states, and general insecurity. IDPs live in jungle camps, monasteries, schools, and border areas — with minimal humanitarian access. The SAC restricts access to conflict areas, preventing aid delivery. UNHCR and NGOs struggle to reach IDPs. Cross-border flight to Thailand, India, and China has increased, with border countries facing pressure from refugees.
laws.penalty: IDPs in conflict areas: subject to military operations; returning IDPs to SAC-controlled areas: risk of detention and interrogation; IDPs providing information to international organizations: risk of informant identification
exceptions: Monastery-based IDP camps have some protection from direct military attack due to religious sensitivity
Thai-Myanmar border crossings have operated informally allowing some civilian flight — though Thailand has periods of forcible return

quiz.q: What factors have driven Myanmar's displacement to over 2 million people?
options: Only economic migration — people seeking better jobs
Exclusively Rohingya persecution in Rakhine State
Multiple causes: village burning in Sagaing/Magway/Chin, fighting between SAC and resistance forces, ethnic conflicts, and general insecurity
Natural disasters exclusively
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's displacement crisis is driven by multiple intersecting causes: SAC military operations burning villages in central Myanmar (Sagaing, Magway, Chin, Kayah), fighting between the military and resistance forces, ethnic conflicts in Rakhine and Shan, and general insecurity. Unlike the earlier Rohingya displacement (which was geographically concentrated), post-coup displacement is nationwide — affecting the ethnic Burman heartland of Myanmar for the first time in decades of armed conflict.

laws.title: Ruby and Gemstone Trade
laws.subtitle: Mogok Valley and International Sanctions
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Mogok Valley is one of the world's most important sources of rubies — the famous pigeon-blood red Mogok rubies command the highest prices globally. The Mong Hsu area produces lower-quality rubies. Sapphires and spinel are also found. The gemstone trade is controlled by military-connected companies and subject to complex revenue flows to the SAC. The US banned imports of Myanmar gems under the Tom Lantos Block Burmese JADE Act (2008) and post-coup sanctions. European markets have also restricted Myanmar gemstone imports. However, gems continue flowing through intermediaries — particularly Dubai and Thailand — obscuring Myanmar origin. Global luxury brands use Myanmar rubies despite restrictions.
laws.penalty: Gemstone trading without SAC license: criminal prosecution; gem smuggling: imprisonment and confiscation; failure to sell to licensed buyer at official price: criminal penalties
exceptions: EAO-controlled gemstone mining areas operate under local governance — outside SAC licensing
Certified pre-2021 stocks of Myanmar rubies can be sold in some markets with provenance documentation

quiz.q: What legislation did the US pass specifically targeting Myanmar gemstone imports?
options: The Burma Sanctions Reform Act
The Asian Gems Protection Law
The Tom Lantos Block Burmese JADE Act (2008) — banning US imports of Myanmar jade and gems
The Myanmar Democracy Support Act
quiz.explanation: The Tom Lantos Block Burmese JADE Act (named for Congressman Tom Lantos) was passed by the US Congress in 2008 — specifically banning imports of jadeite, rubies, and other gems mined or processed in Myanmar from entering the United States. The law was designed to cut off a significant revenue source for the military government. The 'JADE' acronym stands for 'Junta's Anti-Democratic Efforts' — a clever legislative name that signals the law's political purpose.

laws.title: Buddhism and Political Power
laws.subtitle: 969 Movement and Buddhist Nationalism
laws.fullDescription: Buddhism is the dominant religion in Myanmar (87% of the population) and has complex political dimensions. The '969 Movement' led by monk Ashin Wirathu promoted Buddhist nationalist exclusion of Muslims, contributing to anti-Rohingya violence. The state and Sangha (monk community) have historically been intertwined — military governments have sought Buddhist legitimacy. However, many monks opposed the coup — the 2007 Saffron Revolution was led by Buddhist monks. After the coup, some monks joined CDM; others were arrested. Buddhist nationalist extremists have had complex relationships with both the military and anti-Muslim violence that the military has sometimes tolerated or encouraged.
laws.penalty: Monks participating in CDM or anti-coup activity: arrest and disrobing; 'un-Buddhist' political activity per state definition: prosecution; interfaith religious activity without approval: monitoring
exceptions: Senior abbots of major monasteries have some protection from direct arrest due to religious sensitivity
Foreign Buddhist visitors have greater latitude than citizen monks — though monitoring occurs

quiz.q: What was the 2007 Saffron Revolution in Myanmar?
options: A pro-military religious movement
Buddhist monk-led protests against the military government — named for the saffron color of monks' robes
A movement promoting saffron cultivation
A religious revival focused on Buddhist texts
quiz.explanation: The 2007 Saffron Revolution was a series of anti-government protests in Myanmar led primarily by Buddhist monks — named for the saffron color of their robes. The protests began in response to sudden fuel price increases and escalated into broader demands for democratic reform. The military government cracked down violently, arresting hundreds of monks and killing protesters. The Saffron Revolution demonstrated both the political power of Myanmar's Buddhist community and the military's willingness to violently suppress religious-led dissent.

laws.title: Airstrikes on Civilian Areas
laws.subtitle: Targeting Schools, Hospitals, and Villages
laws.fullDescription: The SAC military has conducted systematic airstrikes on civilian areas — schools, hospitals, churches, and villages — as a counter-insurgency tactic. OHCHR documented hundreds of airstrikes on civilian targets. In April 2023, an airstrike on a concert in Pa Zi Gyi village (Kachin State) killed 170+ people including children — one of the worst single attacks of the post-coup conflict. Military jets, helicopters, and light aircraft have all been used. Jet fuel supply restrictions — including US measures targeting military aviation fuel — have had some impact but not stopped aerial operations. The airstrikes are widely documented as violations of international humanitarian law.
laws.penalty: International law: airstrikes on civilian targets are war crimes; SAC domestic law: military operations against 'terrorists' are authorized — no accountability; survivors documenting attacks: terrorism charges possible
exceptions: No effective deterrent mechanism exists to prevent SAC airstrikes on civilians
Satellite imagery and open-source investigation have documented attacks — creating evidentiary record for eventual accountability

quiz.q: What happened at Pa Zi Gyi village in April 2023?
options: A major PDF victory capturing a SAC military base
An SAC airstrike on a concert killed 170+ people including children — one of the war's worst single incidents
A cyclone caused mass displacement
A ceasefire negotiation took place
quiz.explanation: On April 11, 2023, a SAC airstrike struck a public concert in Pa Zi Gyi village in Kachin State — killing over 170 people including children and village elders. The attack targeted a public celebration, not a military installation. The massacre provoked international condemnation and demonstrated the pattern of SAC aerial attacks on civilian gatherings. Investigators determined the attack used military jets and was deliberately targeted at a civilian event.

laws.title: Biodiversity and Wildlife Trafficking
laws.subtitle: Elephants, Tigers, and the Golden Triangle Trade
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar hosts extraordinary biodiversity — Asian elephants, tigers, clouded leopards, tapirs, and numerous endemic species. The country sits astride key wildlife trafficking routes between Southeast Asia and Chinese markets. Mong La (Shan State, controlled by NDAA) is a notorious wildlife trade hub — ivory, tiger parts, bear bile, pangolins, and other protected species sold openly. The combination of weak governance, corrupt border officials, armed group involvement in trafficking, and Chinese demand creates a severe conservation crisis. WWF and WCS had programs in Myanmar pre-coup; most have been suspended. Elephant populations have declined through habitat loss and capture for logging and tourism.
laws.penalty: Wildlife trafficking: criminal prosecution in SAC-controlled areas (rarely enforced in Shan border areas); poaching of protected species: imprisonment; ivory trade: restricted under international CITES obligations
exceptions: Traditional use of certain wildlife for subsistence in remote communities: some tolerance
Buddhist monastery elephants have protected status — cultural practice recognized

quiz.q: What makes Mong La (Shan State, Myanmar) notorious in wildlife conservation?
options: It is a major protected wildlife sanctuary
It is a notorious wildlife trade hub — ivory, tiger parts, pangolins and other species sold openly despite international prohibition
It is the site of Myanmar's last tiger breeding population
It produces Myanmar's legal wildlife medicines
quiz.explanation: Mong La, controlled by the NDAA (National Democratic Alliance Army) in eastern Shan State, has gained international notoriety as an open wildlife trade hub where ivory, tiger parts, bear bile, and other protected species are sold openly in markets. The area's position in the Golden Triangle border zone, outside effective SAC control, makes enforcement virtually impossible. Chinese buyers are the primary customers, driving demand for critically endangered species.

laws.title: ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus
laws.subtitle: Regional Diplomacy and Failure of Engagement
laws.fullDescription: ASEAN (Association of Southeast Asian Nations) adopted a 'Five-Point Consensus' in April 2021 to address the Myanmar crisis: (1) immediate cessation of violence; (2) dialogue among all parties; (3) special envoy appointment; (4) humanitarian assistance; (5) envoy visit to Myanmar. The SAC has systematically failed to implement the consensus — refusing to engage with the NUG and executing political prisoners in violation of point 1. ASEAN has responded by barring SAC political representatives from summits (not technical meetings). The Five-Point Consensus is widely criticized as having given the SAC legitimacy without results, and illustrates the limits of ASEAN's non-interference principle.
laws.penalty: Under ASEAN framework: no enforcement mechanism; SAC non-compliance: diplomatic exclusion from some (not all) ASEAN political meetings
exceptions: ASEAN technical working groups continue interacting with SAC officials on non-political matters
Some ASEAN members (Thailand, Cambodia, Laos) maintain closer ties with SAC than others (Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore)

quiz.q: What has been the international assessment of ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus on Myanmar?
options: It has been highly successful — substantially reducing violence
A qualified success — reducing violence in Rakhine State only
Widely criticized as a failure — the SAC has not implemented it, and the framework gave legitimacy without results
Too early to evaluate — implementation is ongoing
quiz.explanation: ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus has been widely criticized as ineffective. The SAC has systematically failed to implement any of the five points — violence has increased, no genuine dialogue has occurred with the NUG, and the SAC executed political prisoners in direct violation of the agreed ceasefire commitment. Critics argue the consensus provided the SAC with diplomatic cover while the junta continued its campaign of violence.

laws.title: Agriculture and Food Security
laws.subtitle: Rice, Pulses, and Export Disruption
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar is one of Asia's major rice exporters — 'the rice bowl of Asia' historically. Agriculture supports 70% of the rural population. Since the coup, agricultural sector has been severely disrupted: conflict in central Myanmar's Sagaing and Magway regions (key agricultural areas) has displaced farmers, destroyed crops, and disrupted supply chains. Banking system collapse prevents credit for seed and fertilizer purchase. Fuel prices for irrigation have increased. The military has burned granaries and crops in conflict areas as a scorched-earth tactic. WFP estimates food insecurity has dramatically increased. Myanmar's rice exports have declined though exports to China continue.
laws.penalty: Selling crops without SAC permit to unauthorized buyers: criminal prosecution; hoarding during shortage: criminal punishment; farming in conflict areas: extreme danger from all armed parties
exceptions: Subsistence farming for family consumption: generally not criminalized
UN/NGO food assistance programs operate under humanitarian access arrangements

quiz.q: How has the Myanmar military disrupted agriculture in areas of conflict resistance?
options: By imposing protective agricultural tariffs
By burning granaries and crops as a scorched-earth tactic — denying food resources to resistance communities
By nationalizing all rice production
By flooding agricultural land
quiz.explanation: The SAC has employed scorched-earth agricultural destruction as a deliberate military tactic in areas with strong resistance — burning rice granaries, destroying crops, and displacing farming communities to deny food resources to PDF fighters and supportive civilian populations. This tactic, a war crime under international humanitarian law, has severely worsened food insecurity in central Myanmar's Sagaing and Magway regions — the country's agricultural heartland.

laws.title: National Unity Government
laws.subtitle: NUG as Legitimate Alternative Government
laws.fullDescription: The National Unity Government (NUG), formed April 2021 by CRPH members, elected NLD representatives, ethnic political parties, and civil society representatives, claims to be the legitimate government of Myanmar. The NUG has a cabinet structure, issues policy statements, raised international funds (through diaspora), and established the PDF armed wing. No country has formally recognized the NUG as the legitimate government of Myanmar, though many interact with it and treat SAC as illegitimate. The NUG operates primarily from exile (Thailand, Europe) and through underground networks inside Myanmar. It has issued a Federal Democracy Charter as a constitutional framework for a post-coup Myanmar.
laws.penalty: NUG membership: death penalty under SAC law; providing financial support to NUG: terrorism charges; displaying NUG flag: imprisonment
exceptions: NUG officials in exile countries operate under host country legal protection
Informal contact with NUG by foreign governments does not constitute formal recognition

quiz.q: Has any country formally recognized the NUG as Myanmar's legitimate government?
options: Yes — the United States recognized the NUG in 2022
Yes — all EU member states recognized the NUG
No country has formally recognized the NUG — though many interact with it and treat the SAC as illegitimate
China recognized the NUG while ASEAN recognized the SAC
quiz.explanation: Despite its strong democratic credentials — drawing on elected MPs from the 2020 landslide election — no country has formally recognized the NUG as Myanmar's government. Countries face the 'recognition dilemma': formally recognizing the NUG could complicate diplomacy while the SAC controls Naypyidaw and major cities, but legitimizing the SAC rewards the coup. Most democratic countries have chosen a middle path: refusing to recognize the SAC while engaging informally with the NUG.

laws.title: Mental Health and Trauma
laws.subtitle: Post-Coup Psychological Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's population faces a profound mental health crisis following the coup and resulting civil war. Millions have experienced direct violence, displacement, loss of family members, economic desperation, and pervasive fear. The CDM included mental health professionals who left public service; the healthcare system that previously provided limited mental health support has largely collapsed. Rural populations experiencing military operations face acute trauma without any professional support. Buddhist monks and community networks provide informal support but cannot address clinical needs. International NGOs (IRC, IMC) provide some mental health services but access is severely limited in conflict areas.
laws.penalty: Under SAC: mental health treatment by unlicensed practitioners: criminal prosecution; unauthorized psychiatric practice: criminal penalty; no specific mental health law protections for patients
exceptions: ICRC and MSF mental health programs for conflict-affected populations operate under humanitarian access
Buddhist community counseling and support is widely practiced without formal licensing requirements

quiz.q: What informal mental health support system remains functional across Myanmar despite the healthcare collapse?
options: Military-provided psychiatric services
Telemedicine from Bangkok hospitals
Buddhist monks and community networks providing traditional support
Factory counselors for garment workers
quiz.explanation: Buddhist monks and community networks — including extended family structures and village solidarity systems — provide Myanmar's primary informal mental health support following the healthcare system's collapse. While unable to address clinical conditions, these community resources provide social connection, spiritual support, and practical assistance to trauma-affected populations. The CDM's evacuation of medical professionals means formal mental health services are available mainly through the limited programs of international NGOs.

laws.title: Irrawaddy River and Dam Projects
laws.subtitle: Chinese Dams, Fish, and Environmental Trade-offs
laws.fullDescription: The Irrawaddy (Ayeyarwady) River — Myanmar's largest and most culturally significant river — faces multiple environmental threats. Chinese-backed dam projects on the upper Irrawaddy were cancelled (Myitsone Dam, 2011 suspension) but others proceed. The dam at Myitsone would have flooded Kachin cultural heartlands and diverted 90% of river flow to China. Downstream fisheries — supporting millions of livelihoods — are threatened by upstream dam development, sedimentation, and water abstraction. Irrawaddy dolphins (a critically endangered freshwater species found only in the Irrawaddy and a few other rivers) face extinction from fishing nets and water quality decline. Post-coup, environmental governance is essentially non-existent.
laws.penalty: Under SAC: illegal sand mining from Irrawaddy (major activity): inconsistent enforcement; fishing without license: fines; dam operation violations: no practical enforcement
exceptions: Traditional fishing rights by riparian communities: customary practice recognized in some areas
UNESCO World Heritage nominations for Irrawaddy dolphin habitat provide some international advocacy protection

quiz.q: Why was the Myitsone Dam project controversial in Myanmar?
options: It would have flooded Buddhist temples
It would have flooded Kachin cultural heartlands and diverted 90% of the Irrawaddy's flow to China — generating electricity for China while devastating Myanmar
Environmental groups opposed the salmon species displacement
It would have required relocation of only 12 villages
quiz.explanation: The Myitsone Dam was controversial because its design would have diverted approximately 90% of the upper Irrawaddy River's flow through a tunnel to China for hydroelectric power generation — while flooding the confluence of the Irrawaddy's source rivers in Kachin's cultural heartland. Myanmar would have received minimal electricity benefit while bearing all environmental and cultural costs. President Thein Sein suspended the project in 2011 following public outcry — one of the early democratic reform signals.

laws.title: Terrorism Legislation Weaponization
laws.subtitle: Counter-Terrorism Law Against Civilians
laws.fullDescription: The SAC has used Myanmar's Counter-Terrorism Law (CTL) and the Unlawful Associations Act to criminalize virtually all forms of opposition. The NUG, PDF, and most ethnic armed organizations have been designated terrorist organizations — making any contact, support, or association criminal. Journalists who contact designated organizations face terrorism charges. Humanitarian workers providing aid in PDF-controlled areas face terrorism charges. Lawyers who represent political prisoners face disbarment and arrest. The terrorism designation is applied retroactively — prior contact with NLD politicians or EAO members can be grounds for prosecution.
laws.penalty: Association with designated organizations (NUG, PDF, most EAOs): death penalty possible; providing material support: lengthy imprisonment; failing to report suspicious activity: imprisonment
exceptions: UN humanitarian workers have some protection under immunity provisions — though this has been contested in practice
ICRC has framework protections for medical neutrality though these are not consistently respected

quiz.q: What legal consequence does a Myanmar journalist face for contacting the NUG for an interview?
options: No legal consequence — press freedom is protected
A minor reporting violation
Potential terrorism charges — since the NUG is designated a terrorist organization by the SAC
Only a permit violation — unauthorized interview
quiz.explanation: Since the SAC has designated the NUG as a terrorist organization, journalists who contact NUG officials for interviews face potential terrorism charges under Myanmar's Counter-Terrorism Law. This makes independent reporting on the largest opposition group in Myanmar technically a capital offense. The terrorism designation has effectively made truthful reporting on the conflict impossible from inside Myanmar without extreme legal risk.

laws.title: Kachin State Conflict
laws.subtitle: KIA and 10+ Year Resumed Civil War
laws.fullDescription: The Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and its political wing KIO (Kachin Independence Organisation) have fought for Kachin autonomy since 1961. A 1994 ceasefire lasted until 2011, when the military attacked KIA positions in breach of the agreement. Since 2011 (and accelerating after 2021), Kachin State has been in active conflict. The KIA has aligned with the NUG and PDF post-coup. Kachin State hosts important natural resources: jade (Hpakant), amber (the world's most important Cretaceous amber source), gold, and timber. Civilians face displacement, military operations, and humanitarian access restrictions. The church — Kachin are predominantly Christian — provides community support and advocacy.
laws.penalty: Kachin civilians in conflict areas: subject to military operations; contacts with KIA: terrorism charges; participating in Kachin cultural or religious events in conflict zones: risk of military targeting
exceptions: KIA-controlled areas operate under KIO governance systems independent of SAC law
Christian churches provide some community protection through international attention to Kachin Christian community

quiz.q: What makes Kachin State (Myanmar) globally unique in paleontology?
options: It contains the world's largest dinosaur skeleton
Kachin amber deposits are the world's most important source of Cretaceous amber — preserving ancient insects and small animals with extraordinary detail
It has the oldest human remains in Southeast Asia
It contains pre-Cambrian fossil beds
quiz.explanation: Kachin State's amber deposits — mined in the Hukawng Valley — are the world's most important source of Cretaceous amber (approximately 99 million years old). The amber has preserved extraordinary specimens of insects, spiders, feathered dinosaur fragments, and even ancient snakes in three-dimensional detail, revolutionizing paleontology. Tragically, the amber is mined alongside jade in conflict-affected areas — with specimens sometimes mined under dangerous conditions and sold through unethical channels.

laws.title: International Sanctions Regime
laws.subtitle: US, EU, UK, and Australian Sanctions on SAC
laws.fullDescription: Following the coup, the US, EU, UK, Canada, and Australia imposed sanctions targeting SAC military leaders (travel bans, asset freezes), military-connected businesses (MEHL, MEC — the military conglomerates), and the arms trade. US sanctions target Myanmar's gemstone sector, timber, and key SAC officials. EU sanctions have also targeted specific individuals and defense companies. However, major trading partners (China, India, Thailand, ASEAN countries) have not imposed sanctions — significantly limiting their economic impact. Russia and China have continued supplying military equipment to the SAC. The SAC has moved assets to evade sanctions, used front companies, and relied on non-sanctioning countries.
laws.penalty: Sanctions violations by Western companies: criminal prosecution in home country; SAC-designated entities trading with sanctioned parties: secondary sanctions risk; Myanmar persons in sanctioned entities: travel bans and asset freezes in sanctioning countries
exceptions: Humanitarian aid transactions have explicit sanctions carve-outs — food, medicine, and NGO operations continue
Pre-existing contracts have had phase-out periods with specific wind-down authorizations

quiz.q: Why have Western sanctions on Myanmar had limited economic impact on the SAC?
options: The sanctions are not comprehensive enough
The SAC has too many domestic resources
Major trading partners — China, India, Thailand, ASEAN — have not imposed sanctions, providing the SAC with economic lifelines
Myanmar has developed domestic replacements for all sanctioned goods
quiz.explanation: Western sanctions on Myanmar have had limited impact because the major economies that matter most to Myanmar's trade — China, India, Thailand, and ASEAN member states — have not imposed sanctions. China alone accounts for a massive share of Myanmar trade, investment, and military supply. Russia supplies jet fuel and weapons. As long as these major partners continue engagement, Western sanctions reduce but cannot cripple the SAC's economic position.

laws.title: Women's Role in the Resistance
laws.subtitle: Female Activists, Fighters, and Leaders
laws.fullDescription: Women have played an extraordinary role in Myanmar's resistance to the coup. Women were among the first and most prominent protesters — including 'flash mob' protests and the iconic images of women in traditional dress standing in front of military trucks. Women joined the PDF as fighters — some EAOs (particularly the Karen National Liberation Army — KNLA) have long had female fighters. Women lead underground networks, underground schools, and civil society support systems. NUG ministers include women. The resistance has generated discussions about women's expanded role in post-coup Myanmar politics — though traditional gender expectations persist in some ethnic communities.
laws.penalty: Female protesters: arrest, torture, and rape in detention documented; women fighters captured by SAC: severe punishment including sexual violence; female PDF members: death penalty if captured
exceptions: Women in ethnic minority areas with long traditions of female autonomy (some Kachin, Karen communities) face somewhat different social norms
Female foreign nationals participating in advocacy abroad are protected under host country laws

quiz.q: What notable role have women played in the Myanmar post-coup resistance?
options: Women have been largely absent from the resistance
Only older women — not young women — have participated
Extraordinary role — among the first prominent protesters, joining PDF as fighters, leading underground networks, and holding NUG cabinet positions
Only elite women with political connections have participated
quiz.explanation: Women have played an extraordinarily prominent role in Myanmar's resistance to the 2021 coup — from the iconic early protest images of women in traditional dress blocking military vehicles, to joining the PDF as fighters (particularly in Karen units with long traditions of female combatants), to leading underground civil society networks, to holding positions in the NUG cabinet. The resistance has been significantly shaped by women's leadership and participation across all sectors.

laws.title: Cybercrime Law and Digital Control
laws.subtitle: Electronic Transactions Law and Online Arrests
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Electronic Transactions Law (2004, amended 2021) — particularly Section 38 — criminalizes online content that 'affects the stability of the state' or is 'harmful' to society. Post-coup amendments dramatically expanded criminal liability for digital speech. The SAC has arrested hundreds for Facebook posts, WhatsApp messages, and other online activity — charging them with incitement (Section 505a of the Penal Code), defamation of the military, and telecommunications violations. Sentences range from 1-3 years for social media posts to longer terms for organizing through digital channels. The SAC monitors digital communications through seized telecommunications infrastructure.
laws.penalty: Facebook posts critical of SAC: 1-3 years imprisonment; organizing protests online: 3-7 years; defaming military: criminal prosecution; sharing conflict videos: terrorism charges possible
exceptions: Encrypted communications (Signal, Telegram with disappearing messages) provide some protection — though phone seizures at checkpoints expose message history
VPN use is widespread and not directly criminalized — though phone searches at checkpoints reveal VPN use

quiz.q: What section of Myanmar law is most commonly used to prosecute social media posts?
options: Section 18 of the Internet Safety Law
Section 505(a) of the Penal Code — incitement — applied to anti-coup social media content
Article 12 of the Broadcasting Law
Section 66(d) of the Telecommunications Law for defamation
quiz.explanation: Section 505(a) of Myanmar's Penal Code — criminalizing statements that cause fear or alarm or incite offenses against the state — is the most commonly used charge against social media users and protesters. The SAC has applied this provision broadly to anyone posting anti-coup content. Combined with Section 38 of the Electronic Transactions Law (harmful online content), these two provisions have been used to imprison hundreds for social media posts.

laws.title: Mangrove Destruction and Coastal Ecosystems
laws.subtitle: Aquaculture, Logging, and Climate Vulnerability
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Ayeyarwady Delta and Rakhine coast contain some of Southeast Asia's largest remaining mangrove ecosystems. Mangroves provide essential services: storm surge protection (critical given Myanmar's cyclone exposure), fish nursery habitat (supporting coastal fishing communities), carbon sequestration, and coastal stabilization. Mangrove destruction has accelerated from aquaculture (shrimp farms), charcoal production, and rice paddy expansion. Cyclone Nargis (2008) devastated mangroves that had previously reduced storm surge damage. Under the SAC, environmental governance is non-functional. Climate change increases the urgency of mangrove protection — but post-coup, conservation organizations have withdrawn.
laws.penalty: Illegal mangrove clearing: criminal prosecution under Forestry Law (rarely enforced); aquaculture in protected mangrove areas: fines
exceptions: Traditional mangrove-dependent fishing communities have customary use rights — generally recognized
Emergency mangrove charcoal for cooking fuel in displaced communities: tolerated as survival necessity

quiz.q: What protection do mangroves provide that Cyclone Nargis dramatically demonstrated?
options: They prevent coastal earthquakes
Storm surge reduction — intact mangroves significantly reduce cyclone damage to coastal communities
They provide fish protein for coastal communities exclusively
They prevent salt water intrusion into freshwater aquifers
quiz.explanation: Cyclone Nargis (2008) — the deadliest natural disaster in Myanmar's history, killing 140,000 people — demonstrated the protective value of mangroves. Areas where mangroves had been cleared for shrimp farms suffered far greater storm surge damage than areas with intact mangrove belts. The comparison provided powerful evidence that mangrove destruction increases cyclone mortality — making mangrove conservation a life-safety issue, not just an ecological preference.

laws.title: Education System Destruction
laws.subtitle: CDM Teachers and Underground Schools
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's education system has been severely damaged since the coup. Teachers joined the CDM en masse — leaving government schools largely non-functional. The SAC hired replacement teachers but quality and coverage are inadequate. Many parents refuse to send children to SAC-controlled schools — seeing them as instruments of indoctrination. In conflict areas, schools have been attacked and occupied by the military (documented by OHCHR). Underground schools — operating in monasteries, homes, and border areas — serve displaced children. Some EAO-controlled areas maintain their own school systems. Generation-level education losses are accumulating — particularly in conflict-affected rural areas.
laws.penalty: Teaching in unauthorized schools: arrest and imprisonment; providing CDM education support: criminal charges; attending NUG-affiliated educational programs: classified as supporting terrorism
exceptions: Monastery-based schools have some protection due to religious significance
UNICEF educational programs operate under humanitarian access — typically in less conflict-affected areas

quiz.q: Why do many Myanmar parents refuse to send children to SAC-controlled schools?
options: Schools are too far from their villages
School fees are unaffordable
They view SAC schools as instruments of military indoctrination — and many prefer CDM teachers in underground schools
Schools are physically unsafe due to poor construction
quiz.explanation: Many Myanmar parents refuse to send children to SAC-controlled government schools because they view them as instruments of military indoctrination — teaching pro-junta content and normalizing military governance. This resistance has led families to prefer underground schools run by CDM teachers, which often operate in monasteries, private homes, and displacement camps. While these underground schools provide better values alignment, they typically lack resources, materials, and stable premises.

laws.title: Garment Industry and Labor Rights
laws.subtitle: Factory Workers and Western Brand Sourcing
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's garment industry — employing hundreds of thousands of mostly female workers — was a growing export sector supplying Western brands before the coup. Many brands (H&M, Inditex, Primark, Marks & Spencer) exited Myanmar following the coup due to human rights concerns and sourcing policies. Factory workers lost jobs as brands departed. Some factories remain operating (supplying brands without public sourcing policies). Labor unions, which had made progress under democratic governments, were suppressed. Strike activity was cracked down. Workers face the choice between employment in SAC-normalized factories or poverty from unemployment.
laws.penalty: Trade union organizing: arrest and imprisonment post-coup; strikes: criminal prosecution; labor advocacy: terrorism charges possible
exceptions: ILO (International Labour Organization) maintains some presence in Myanmar under longstanding special framework — though severely constrained
Workers in remaining factories have extremely limited labor rights protection

quiz.q: Why did many Western fashion brands exit Myanmar after the coup?
options: Myanmar garments became too expensive compared to Bangladesh
Trade sanctions made import impossible
Human rights concerns — brands' sourcing policies required exiting suppliers in countries with systematic human rights violations
Quality standards in Myanmar garments declined
quiz.explanation: Major Western fashion brands exited Myanmar following the coup due to their own sourcing policies and investor/consumer pressure — recognizing that purchasing Myanmar garments generated revenue flowing (through taxes and economic activity) to the SAC junta. Brands including H&M, Primark, Marks & Spencer, and others concluded that continued sourcing was incompatible with their human rights commitments. The exit caused significant hardship for garment workers who lost employment.

laws.title: Naypyidaw — Capital and Military City
laws.subtitle: Planned Capital and SAC Governance Center
laws.fullDescription: Naypyidaw — Myanmar's purpose-built capital, constructed from 2002-2006 by the military government under Than Shwe — is the administrative center of the SAC. Located in central Myanmar away from major population centers, Naypyidaw was designed for military control: wide boulevards for military vehicles, government ministries with blast-proof buildings, military hospitals, and large parade grounds. The capital was maintained by the SAC after the coup as the seat of government. Unlike Yangon (the commercial capital), Naypyidaw has minimal civilian population — making it less vulnerable to protest. The SAC has constructed additional defense infrastructure around Naypyidaw since the coup.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized access to government zone: arrest; protest in Naypyidaw area: extreme risk — heavy SAC security presence; foreign journalist access: requires SAC authorization
exceptions: Diplomatic missions (embassy zone) continue operating under diplomatic immunity
UN agencies with formal SAC accreditation have limited access to Naypyidaw government facilities

quiz.q: Why was Myanmar's capital moved from Yangon to Naypyidaw?
options: Yangon was vulnerable to flooding from rising sea levels
For national development and decentralization
Primarily for military strategic reasons — the military wanted a defensible capital away from the coast and population centers, better suited for military vehicle movement
For economic development of the central region
