quiz.explanation: Myanmar's military government moved the capital from Yangon to the purpose-built Naypyidaw primarily for strategic military reasons. Senior General Than Shwe reportedly wanted a defensible capital away from the coast (reducing vulnerability to naval attack), away from large civilian populations (reducing protest risk), and designed for military control — with wide boulevards for military vehicle movement and blast-proof government buildings. Naypyidaw's remote inland location makes it more defensible than the coastal, populous Yangon.

laws.title: HIV and Drug-Related Health Crisis
laws.subtitle: Intravenous Drug Use and AIDS in Shan State
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has one of Asia's highest HIV rates — concentrated among intravenous drug users (particularly in Shan and Kachin states adjacent to opium-producing areas), sex workers, and men who have sex with men (MSM). UNAIDS estimates 240,000+ people living with HIV in Myanmar. Harm reduction programs (needle exchange, opioid substitution therapy) that had been established under previous governments have been disrupted post-coup. MSF and partners provide HIV treatment in conflict areas under dangerous conditions. The combination of widespread drug use, sexual exploitation, and healthcare collapse creates conditions for HIV transmission increase. LGBTQ+ people face additional persecution under SAC — complicating MSM-focused HIV prevention.
laws.penalty: Intravenous drug use: arrest and imprisonment; HIV-positive status is not directly criminalized but HIV-related activities (sex work, drug use) are; harm reduction program operation without SAC authorization: criminal risk
exceptions: MSF and international medical organizations provide HIV treatment under humanitarian access protocols
WHO HIV program maintains some operations through limited SAC engagement

quiz.q: Which populations in Myanmar bear the greatest burden of HIV?
options: Urban business professionals
Agricultural workers in the delta
Intravenous drug users in Shan/Kachin states, sex workers, and MSM — populations concentrated near opium-producing border regions
Only Rohingya communities in Rakhine State
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's HIV epidemic is concentrated primarily in intravenous drug users (particularly in the opium-producing Shan and Kachin regions where cheap heroin is widely available), sex workers, and MSM (men who have sex with men). These populations face criminalization of their risk behaviors, stigma, and limited healthcare access — creating conditions for HIV transmission. The post-coup healthcare collapse has severely disrupted antiretroviral treatment and harm reduction programs.

laws.title: Village Burning as Military Tactic
laws.subtitle: Scorched Earth in Resistance Areas
laws.fullDescription: The SAC military has burned hundreds of villages since the coup — primarily in Sagaing, Magway, Chin, Karen, and Kayah states where resistance is strongest. Village burnings are used as collective punishment against communities perceived to support the PDF, to create buffer zones, and to displace civilian populations that provide cover for guerrilla fighters. Satellite analysis by independent researchers (Myanmar Witness, ACLED) has documented over 60,000 destroyed or damaged structures. The military uses helicopters, ground troops, and arson to destroy villages. Civilians are sometimes killed or taken during village-burning operations.
laws.penalty: International law: deliberate destruction of civilian property and collective punishment are war crimes; SAC domestic law: military operations against 'terrorist-supporting' villages are authorized — no accountability
exceptions: Satellite documentation and open-source investigation create evidentiary record for future accountability proceedings
UN Special Rapporteur reports document specific incidents — building international pressure

quiz.q: Approximately how many structures have been destroyed or damaged in Myanmar village burnings since the coup?
options: About 5,000
Around 15,000
Over 60,000 — documented by satellite analysis
The number is unknown — no documentation is possible
quiz.explanation: Independent researchers using satellite imagery — including Myanmar Witness and ACLED (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data) — have documented over 60,000 destroyed or damaged structures in Myanmar since the 2021 coup. This extraordinary figure reflects systematic SAC village burning across multiple states as a counter-insurgency tactic. The scale of destruction rivals or exceeds many recognized humanitarian emergencies, yet has received relatively limited international attention compared to other conflicts.

laws.title: Myanmar in ASEAN Regional Context
laws.subtitle: Strategic Importance and Regional Dynamics
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar occupies a critical strategic position: land bridge between South and Southeast Asia, sharing borders with China, India, Thailand, Laos, and Bangladesh. China has significant economic interests (pipelines, infrastructure, border trade) and considers Myanmar within its sphere of influence. India competes with China for Myanmar influence — strategic interests include connectivity to Southeast Asia and concern about Chinese encirclement. Thailand hosts the largest Myanmar refugee population outside Bangladesh and is the primary destination for economic migrants. ASEAN membership gives Myanmar a formal regional institutional framework, though one without effective enforcement mechanisms. The coup has repositioned Myanmar as a destabilizing factor in Southeast Asian geopolitics.
laws.penalty: No formal legal framework for Myanmar's regional relationships; bilateral disputes managed through diplomacy; cross-border military incidents: bilateral diplomatic protests
exceptions: ASEAN institutional frameworks provide some dispute management mechanisms
Bilateral investment treaties provide arbitration for commercial disputes

quiz.q: Why does India compete with China for influence in Myanmar?
options: India wants to build oil pipelines through Myanmar
India sees Myanmar as its primary food supplier
India needs Myanmar as a land bridge to Southeast Asia and wants to prevent Chinese strategic encirclement from the east
India and Myanmar have a long historical cultural relationship
quiz.explanation: India views Myanmar as essential for its 'Act East' connectivity policy — providing overland access to Southeast Asia and serving as a critical link in India's effort to counter Chinese strategic influence in its neighborhood. Indian investment in Myanmar infrastructure (the Kaladan Multi-modal Transit Transport project, the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway) reflects this strategic interest. India fears Chinese dominance in Myanmar would allow China to encircle India both to the north (Tibet, Nepal) and east.

laws.title: Mining Law and Resource Extraction
laws.subtitle: SAC Mining Concessions and Environmental Degradation
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has vast mineral wealth — copper (Monywa area), nickel, gold, coal, zinc, lead, and rare earth elements. Mining operations are operated by military-connected companies (UMEHL) and Chinese joint ventures. Environmental standards in mining are minimal — the Monywa copper mine (operated in a joint venture with Chinese company Wanbao) has been associated with land confiscation, pollution, and farmer protests. Since the coup, Chinese companies have expanded mining concessions. Post-coup environmental governance is essentially non-existent. Artisanal mining of gold in river systems is widespread — using mercury with severe health and environmental consequences.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized mining without SAC permit: imprisonment and confiscation; environmental violations from permitted mines: no practical enforcement; mercury use in artisanal gold mining: not effectively regulated
exceptions: EAO-controlled mining areas operate under local governance — outside SAC permitting
Chinese state-owned enterprise mining operations have practical immunity from environmental enforcement

quiz.q: What environmental and health hazard is associated with artisanal gold mining in Myanmar's rivers?
options: Radioactive contamination from naturally occurring uranium
Mercury use — contaminating waterways and creating severe neurological health impacts for miners and downstream communities
Arsenic from gold ore processing
Cyanide leaching into groundwater
quiz.explanation: Artisanal gold miners in Myanmar's rivers use mercury — poured over gold-bearing sediments to amalgamate the gold, then burned off — as a cheap and accessible extraction method. Mercury vapor inhaled during the burning process causes severe neurological damage; mercury released into rivers bioaccumulates in fish and contaminates the water supply for downstream communities. Myanmar is among Asia's significant sources of mercury pollution from artisanal mining, with health impacts spreading well beyond mine sites.

laws.title: Military Court Jurisdiction
laws.subtitle: Civilians Tried in Military Tribunals
laws.fullDescription: Post-coup, the SAC has extended military court jurisdiction over civilians for a wide range of offenses — bypassing the civilian court system. Civilian courts that continue operating face intense pressure and intimidation. Judges who ruled against the military government pre-coup were targeted. Political prisoners face 'military tribunal' proceedings with no independent legal representation, no right to call witnesses, no right to challenge evidence, and no meaningful right of appeal. Death sentences can be issued and implemented without transparent process. Aung San Suu Kyi's multiple trials were conducted in this system — in a specially constructed courtroom inside the detention facility to prevent public observation.
laws.penalty: Military tribunal sentencing: no minimum standards apply; death sentences from military courts: executed after minimal procedural review; civilian court judgments: subject to SAC override
exceptions: Minor civilian cases (contract disputes, some family law matters) continue in civilian courts with some legal process
Foreign nationals in Myanmar face diplomatic protection for consular notification — though not military tribunal exemption
laws.sourceLabel: Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma

quiz.q: Where were Aung San Suu Kyi's post-coup trials conducted?
options: In the Supreme Court of Myanmar — open to public observation
In a specially constructed courtroom inside the detention facility — preventing public observation and legal scrutiny
Via videoconference from her detention location
In the International Court of Justice in The Hague
quiz.explanation: Aung San Suu Kyi's multiple trials were conducted in a specially constructed courtroom inside the Naypyidaw detention facility where she was held — preventing lawyers, family, diplomats, or media from observing proceedings. This design ensured that no independent verification of the 'evidence' or proceedings was possible. Her defense lawyers were subject to restrictions on communication, and their eventual disbarment further compromised her defense.

laws.title: Shan State Complexity
laws.subtitle: Multiple Armed Groups and Ethnic Mosaic
laws.fullDescription: Shan State — Myanmar's largest state, comprising one-third of Myanmar's territory — is an extraordinarily complex patchwork of ethnic groups, armed organizations, and governance systems. Major actors include: RCSS/SSA (Shan State Army — South), SSPP/SSA-North, TNLA (Ta'ang), MNDAA (Kokang), UWSA (Wa — the world's largest non-state military force, with 30,000+ soldiers), Restoration Council factions, and multiple smaller groups. The Wa region is essentially an autonomous zone — with close Chinese ties, its own currency, and no practical SAC authority. Drug production, Chinese economic influence, and ethnic complexity make Shan State arguably the most strategically complex territory in Southeast Asia.
laws.penalty: Shan State residents face jurisdiction of whichever armed actor controls their area — SAC, UWSA, RCSS, MNDAA, or others; moving between zones requires crossing frontlines with associated risks
exceptions: UWSA territory (Wa Special Region) operates entirely outside SAC law — a de facto Chinese-aligned autonomous zone
Cross-border trade with China in MNDAA territory follows Chinese commercial norms rather than Myanmar law

quiz.q: What makes the United Wa State Army (UWSA) remarkable among armed non-state actors?
options: It is Myanmar's oldest armed organization — founded in 1948
The UWSA is the world's largest non-state military force with 30,000+ soldiers — operating a de facto autonomous state with close Chinese ties
The UWSA has achieved a formal ceasefire recognized by the UN
The UWSA is the only ethnic armed organization to have signed the National Ceasefire Agreement
quiz.explanation: The United Wa State Army is remarkable as the world's largest non-state (non-government) military force — with an estimated 30,000+ soldiers, surface-to-air missiles, armored vehicles, and close ties to China. The UWSA controls the Wa Special Region in eastern Shan State — a de facto autonomous territory with its own administration, police, and currency. The UWSA officially banned opium cultivation in 2005 and has sought international recognition as a legitimate political entity.

laws.title: Hawala Banking and Informal Finance
laws.subtitle: Remittances and Informal Value Transfer
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's formal banking system has been severely disrupted post-coup. Banking confidence collapsed after CDM participation by bank employees and SAC seizure of accounts. Banks imposed withdrawal limits. Capital flight by wealthy Burmese drained bank reserves. Formal banking for ordinary citizens became unreliable. The informal hawala/hundi system — traditional South and Southeast Asian value transfer networks — has expanded to fill the gap. Diaspora remittances (Myanmar has significant communities in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan, and Western countries) primarily flow through informal channels. The SAC has attempted to force currency conversion — requiring dollar accounts to convert to kyat at unfavorable official rates.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized foreign currency holding above official limits: criminal prosecution; hawala operation without registration: criminal prosecution (rarely enforced given necessity); dollar-to-kyat exchange at market rates: criminal offense
exceptions: Humanitarian organizations have OFAC/OFSI authorization to use informal transfer systems for aid delivery
Emergency medical expenses may use informal channels under humanitarian exception

quiz.q: What currency policy did the SAC impose that caused economic alarm?
options: Banning all foreign currency accounts
Requiring dollar accounts to convert to kyat at unfavorable official rates — below the actual market rate
Dollarizing the Myanmar economy
Fixing the kyat to the Chinese yuan
quiz.explanation: The SAC ordered forced conversion of foreign currency accounts (particularly US dollars) to kyat at the official exchange rate — which was significantly below the actual market rate. This effectively confiscated a portion of account holders' savings. The policy caused panic bank runs, accelerated capital flight, further destabilized the kyat, and drove more economic activity underground into the informal sector. The policy was widely seen as the SAC raiding bank accounts to fund its military operations.

laws.title: Ethnic Federalism vs. Military Unitarism
laws.subtitle: Federal Democracy Charter and Post-Coup Vision
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's fundamental political conflict — beneath the coup and counter-coup — is the unresolved question of ethnic federalism versus military-enforced unitary state. The Burman-dominated military has consistently resisted genuine ethnic autonomy. Ethnic armed organizations have fought for decades for federal arrangements respecting ethnic identity, territorial control, and self-governance. The NUG's Federal Democracy Charter — drafted in consultation with ethnic organizations — proposes a genuine federal democracy with regional parliaments, land rights, and ethnic protections. This vision is fundamentally incompatible with the Tatmadaw's conception of a unitary Myanmar where the military is the ultimate guarantor of national unity.
laws.penalty: Advocating federalism (in SAC-controlled areas): potentially treated as separatism — criminal prosecution; ethnic rights advocacy: suppressed; displaying ethnic national flags in some areas: risk
exceptions: Ethnic customary law is recognized in practice in EAO-controlled areas — outside SAC legal framework
NUG's Federal Democracy Charter is the operative constitutional framework in liberated areas

quiz.q: What is Myanmar's Federal Democracy Charter?
options: The 2008 military constitution
An ASEAN proposal for Myanmar governance
The NUG's constitutional framework proposing genuine ethnic federalism — drafted with ethnic armed organizations as a post-coup vision for Myanmar
A UN Security Council resolution on Myanmar's governance
quiz.explanation: The Federal Democracy Charter is the NUG's constitutional framework — drafted in consultation with ethnic political parties and armed organizations — proposing to replace Myanmar's unitary military-dominated governance with genuine ethnic federalism. The Charter envisions regional parliaments, ethnic rights protection, land reform, and military restructuring under civilian control. It represents the resistance's vision for Myanmar's political future and has created unprecedented unity between the Burman pro-democracy movement and ethnic armed organizations.

laws.title: Myanmar-China Border Trade
laws.subtitle: Yunnan Province and Commercial Ties
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's northern and eastern border with China's Yunnan Province has been a major commercial corridor for centuries. Border trade — including legal goods and significant informal flows — has continued despite the coup. Chinese companies operate extensively in Kachin and Shan states. The Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State (part of China's Belt and Road Initiative) would give China's Yunnan province access to the Indian Ocean. The China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) infrastructure projects continue. China has maintained close ties with the SAC while also maintaining relationships with key EAOs (particularly UWSA and MNDAA) — a dual-track approach protecting Chinese interests regardless of how the conflict resolves.
laws.penalty: Cross-border trade with China: subject to SAC customs regulations; unauthorized trade: smuggling charges; Chinese investment projects: subject to Chinese-SAC bilateral agreements outside normal Myanmar legal framework
exceptions: Chinese state company investments have special treaty protections under bilateral investment agreements
Humanitarian goods crossing China-Myanmar border: simplified customs procedures during emergencies

quiz.q: What strategic infrastructure project gives China ocean access through Myanmar?
options: The Myitsone Dam hydroelectric project
The Mandalay-Kunming railway connecting Yunnan to central Myanmar
The Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Rakhine State — connecting Yunnan Province to the Indian Ocean via pipeline and port
The Monywa copper mine access road
quiz.explanation: The Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Myanmar's Rakhine State — a key component of China's Belt and Road Initiative — would give China's landlocked Yunnan Province direct access to the Bay of Bengal and Indian Ocean through a port and pipeline. This would allow Chinese oil and gas imports to bypass the Strait of Malacca (a strategic chokepoint) by flowing directly from Rakhine to Yunnan. The project represents China's most strategically significant infrastructure investment in Myanmar.

laws.title: Forest Conservation and Elephant Corridors
laws.subtitle: Myanmar's Biodiversity Corridors
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's forests — the most extensive remaining in mainland Southeast Asia — connect biodiversity corridors from the Eastern Himalayas to the Malay Peninsula. Asian elephants, tigers, and numerous endemic species depend on these corridors. Conservation programs (Wildlife Conservation Society, WWF) operated in Myanmar pre-coup under government cooperation. Post-coup, most international conservation organizations have withdrawn or severely reduced operations. Elephant corridors are increasingly fragmented by conflict, road construction, and encroachment. Myanmar's elephants face capture for logging operations (working elephants in Myanmar's timber industry), and illegal trade to circuses and tourist venues in China and Southeast Asia.
laws.penalty: Elephant poaching or capture without permit: criminal prosecution; ivory trade: restricted under CITES; unauthorized elephant capture for working use: criminal offense in theory — poorly enforced
exceptions: Traditional working elephants in Myanmar's timber industry have a special regulatory category
Captive breeding programs at elephant camps have some regulatory protection

quiz.q: Why are Myanmar's forests particularly significant for wildlife conservation?
options: Myanmar has the world's highest forest biodiversity
Myanmar forests connect corridors from the Eastern Himalayas to the Malay Peninsula — critical linkages for elephant, tiger, and other large mammal populations
Myanmar is the last habitat for Sumatran tigers
Myanmar forests produce 30% of global oxygen
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's forests provide the critical biodiversity corridors connecting the Eastern Himalayas (including Yunnan and the Indo-Burma biodiversity hotspot) to the Malay Peninsula's forests. These connected corridors are essential for Asian elephant, tiger, and other large mammal populations to maintain genetic diversity and seasonal migration. Myanmar's deforestation therefore threatens not just Myanmar's biodiversity but the viability of ecological networks extending across multiple countries.

laws.title: Land Confiscation and Property Rights
laws.subtitle: Military Land Seizures and Displacement
laws.fullDescription: Land confiscation by the Myanmar military has been a persistent grievance for decades — military-connected companies seize agricultural land for plantations, mining, and development without adequate compensation. Post-coup, SAC-connected entities have expanded land seizures. Farmers protesting land confiscation face arrest. Properties of CDM participants and political opponents have been confiscated. The Land Acquisition Act and related laws have been used to 'legally' legitimize military land grabs. In conflict areas, displacement creates de facto land abandonment — with military and armed actors occupying vacated areas. Land grievances are a primary driver of rural support for the resistance.
laws.penalty: Occupying 'state' land without authorization: criminal prosecution; protesting land confiscation: arrest; returning to confiscated land: trespass prosecution; documenting land grabs for international reporting: terrorism charges possible
exceptions: Traditional community land rights recognized in EAO-controlled areas under local governance
Emergency temporary shelter on displaced farmland: tolerated in humanitarian crises

quiz.q: How has land confiscation contributed to the post-coup resistance movement?
options: It has had minimal effect on resistance motivation
Land was confiscated only from elites — not ordinary farmers
Decades of military land grabs have been a primary rural grievance — making communities predisposed to support the resistance, particularly in Sagaing and Magway where resistance is strongest
Land confiscation affected only ethnic minority areas
quiz.explanation: Decades of military land confiscation — seizing agricultural land from farming communities for military-connected plantations, mining, and development projects — created a reservoir of rural grievance against the Tatmadaw. When the coup occurred, communities in Sagaing and Magway (the ethnic Burman heartland where military land grabs were extensive) immediately supported the resistance. Land grievance is identified by conflict analysts as one of the key factors explaining why rural communities risk military violence to support the PDF.

laws.title: Drug Use and Addiction
laws.subtitle: Yaba and Heroin in Myanmar
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar faces a severe domestic drug use crisis alongside its role as a major producer. 'Yaba' (methamphetamine tablets — from the Thai word meaning 'crazy medicine') is widely used — particularly among young people and workers seeking to work longer hours. Cheap heroin in Shan and Kachin states creates local addiction crises. Under the previous government, harm reduction and treatment programs made some progress; post-coup, these have largely collapsed. SAC enforces drug laws through arrest and punishment rather than treatment approaches. Drug use is particularly prevalent in conflict-affected and economically devastated communities.
laws.penalty: Drug use: arrest and imprisonment (typically 1-3 years for first offense); possession with intent: longer imprisonment; trafficking: death penalty
exceptions: Needle exchange programs in some areas operate under UNODC authorization
Medical opiate use in licensed facilities permitted with strict controls

quiz.q: What does 'Yaba' mean and why is the name significant?
options: It means 'white powder' in Burmese — describing the drug's color
It means 'crazy medicine' in Thai — reflecting the drug's stimulant effects that enable extended work
It is a brand name from the original Thai manufacturer
It means 'victory pills' — named by the Thai military for its wartime use
quiz.explanation: 'Yaba' is the Thai word for 'crazy medicine' — a name that captures the methamphetamine tablets' effect of enabling extended work hours and creating a feeling of energy and euphoria, followed by addiction. Originally called 'yama' (horse medicine) in Thailand for use by workers and truck drivers, the drug was rebranded by Thai traffickers as 'yaba' and became the most widely used illicit drug in mainland Southeast Asia. Myanmar's Golden Triangle produces much of the regional supply.

laws.title: Enforced Disappearances
laws.subtitle: Families Without Information
laws.fullDescription: The SAC has conducted systematic enforced disappearances — taking individuals without acknowledgment, providing no information to families about detention location, and in many cases eventually revealing the person died in custody. Enforced disappearance is a crime under international law (International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance). Families who seek information about disappeared relatives risk arrest. The AAPP tracks disappearances. Many CDM participants who went underground to avoid arrest have also 'disappeared' from the perspective of their families — living clandestinely in resistance areas. The total number of enforced disappearances since 2021 is in the thousands.
laws.penalty: Enforced disappearance: international law crime — ICC/ICJ potential liability for commanders; families seeking information: risk of arrest; international reporting on disappearances: terrorism charges possible
exceptions: ICRC requests for information on detained persons have some protection under ICRC's special international status
UN Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances handles cases — though Myanmar SAC does not cooperate
laws.sourceLabel: Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma

quiz.q: What international convention specifically addresses enforced disappearances?
options: The Geneva Convention Additional Protocol III
The UN Convention Against Torture
The International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance
The Rome Statute Article on Disappearances
quiz.explanation: The International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance (adopted 2006, entered force 2010) is the specific international instrument addressing enforced disappearances — defining them as crimes under international law and creating obligations for states to investigate and prosecute them. The convention establishes a Committee on Enforced Disappearances that receives cases. Myanmar has not ratified the convention, but enforced disappearance can also constitute a crime against humanity under the Rome Statute.

laws.title: Bay of Bengal Climate Vulnerability
laws.subtitle: Cyclones, Sea Level Rise, and Delta Communities
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Ayeyarwady Delta and Bay of Bengal coast are among Asia's most climate-vulnerable areas. The delta — home to millions of farmers and fishing communities — sits just above sea level. Cyclone Nargis (2008) killed 140,000 people in the delta in a single storm event. Sea level rise threatens the delta's long-term habitability. Saltwater intrusion is already degrading agricultural land in coastal areas. Stronger cyclones (climate change increases intensity) will cause greater damage as mangroves are removed. Under the SAC, climate adaptation planning is non-existent. Displacement from climate impacts compounds displacement from the conflict.
laws.penalty: No Myanmar climate liability framework; delta farmers losing land to sea level rise: no compensation mechanism; government relocation programs: inconsistent and potentially coercive
exceptions: UN disaster preparedness programs maintain some presence in less conflict-affected delta areas
Traditional community disaster response systems (village-level cyclone preparation) continue operating

quiz.q: What climate event demonstrated the Ayeyarwady Delta's extreme cyclone vulnerability?
options: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami
Typhoon Haiyan in 2013
Cyclone Nargis in 2008 — killing 140,000 people in the delta
Cyclone Amphan in 2020
quiz.explanation: Cyclone Nargis (May 2008) devastated the Ayeyarwady Delta, killing approximately 140,000 people — Myanmar's worst natural disaster in recorded history. The storm surge penetrated 40+ kilometers inland across the flat delta. The military government's initial refusal to allow international aid access (eventually partially reversed) worsened the death toll. Nargis remains one of the deadliest tropical cyclones in history and a stark demonstration of the delta's extreme vulnerability.

laws.title: Refugee Crisis in Thailand
laws.subtitle: 2 Million Myanmar Refugees and Migrants
laws.fullDescription: Thailand hosts approximately 2 million Myanmar migrants and refugees — the largest receiving country outside Bangladesh. Long-standing communities of ethnic Karen, Shan, and Mon in Thai border areas predate the 2021 coup. Post-coup, a new wave of political refugees (NUG officials, CDM participants, journalists, activists) joined economic migrants. Thailand has generally tolerated the presence but maintains a policy of not formally recognizing refugees under the 1951 Convention (Thailand hasn't signed it). Forcible returns to Myanmar occur periodically. Thai authorities have deported high-profile coup opponents. Myanmar migrants in Thailand face exploitation, wage theft, and minimal labor rights — though are vital to Thai agriculture and construction.
laws.penalty: Myanmar refugees in Thailand: non-refoulement theoretically applies — Thailand has not signed Refugee Convention; police raids and detention: documented; deportation of coup opponents: documented despite non-refoulement obligations
exceptions: UNHCR-registered refugees have some protection from deportation in practice
Long-established ethnic minority communities in border areas have complex arrangements with Thai authorities

quiz.q: Why does Thailand not formally recognize Myanmar refugees under international refugee law?
options: Thailand only recognizes refugees from non-Asian countries
Thailand has signed the 1951 Refugee Convention with reservations excluding Myanmar
Thailand has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention — allowing a policy of not formally granting refugee status while tolerating presence
Thailand recognizes all Myanmar refugees automatically
quiz.explanation: Thailand has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol — meaning it has no legal framework for formally granting refugee status. This allows Thailand to maintain a pragmatic policy of tolerating the presence of Myanmar migrants and refugees without the formal rights and protections that come with Convention refugee status. While UNHCR registers refugees in Thailand, the Thai government does not recognize this status — leaving refugees in a legal limbo subject to periodic detention and deportation.

laws.title: Teak Trade and International Ban
laws.subtitle: Myanmar Teak and Sustainable Forestry
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar natural teak — the gold standard for outdoor furniture, boat decking, and construction — was a major export earner for decades. Teak's extraordinary durability, oil content, and beauty made it a premium global commodity. The EU banned Myanmar teak imports following the coup (as part of sanctions). The US also restricts Myanmar timber imports (dating to pre-coup legislation). However, teak continues flowing through intermediaries — processed in Vietnam, China, or India to obscure Myanmar origin before export. The military-controlled MTE (Myanmar Timber Enterprise) controls teak harvesting. International certification bodies (FSC) have suspended Myanmar operations. Sustainable forestry has collapsed.
laws.penalty: Illegal teak logging without MTE permit: criminal prosecution; teak smuggling: imprisonment and confiscation; EU/US sanction violations by importers: criminal prosecution in Europe/US
exceptions: Pre-coup teak stocks with documented chain of custody can be sold in some markets — diminishing supply
Antique teak (pre-prohibition) has separate market rules in many jurisdictions

quiz.q: Why is Myanmar teak considered the gold standard for outdoor applications?
options: It is the cheapest available hardwood
Its extraordinary natural oil content makes it uniquely durable and resistant to weathering, insects, and warping — lasting generations outdoors
It is easily shaped and painted
It has religious significance that increases its commercial value
quiz.explanation: Myanmar teak's extraordinary durability comes from its high natural oil content — which makes the wood naturally water-resistant, insect-resistant, dimensionally stable, and resistant to warping even in harsh outdoor conditions. Teak furniture and boat decks can last decades or generations with minimal maintenance. No other commercially available wood combines teak's durability, workability, and aesthetic qualities — making it irreplaceable for premium outdoor applications despite its high cost.

laws.title: State of Emergency and Rule of Law
laws.subtitle: SAC Emergency Extensions and Governance Crisis
laws.fullDescription: The SAC declared a state of emergency on February 1, 2021 — ostensibly for one year, extendable per the 2008 constitution. The SAC has repeatedly extended the state of emergency — using each extension to delay any transition timetable. Elections promised for within two years of the coup have been repeatedly postponed. The SAC announced 2023 elections but created conditions (new electoral law, new Election Commission, NLD dissolution) that made meaningful participation impossible. All meaningful rule of law has been suspended under the state of emergency. The SAC uses emergency powers to justify all otherwise extraordinary measures — detention, media control, property confiscation, and military courts.
laws.penalty: All actions authorized under state of emergency framework — no independent judicial review; challenging emergency extension: criminal prosecution; organizing for elections: risk of arrest
exceptions: Some commercial and civil law continues operating for non-political matters
Foreign investors with dispute resolution clauses in bilateral investment treaties can pursue international arbitration outside Myanmar courts

quiz.q: What electoral manipulation did the SAC conduct to ensure election results would favor the junta?
options: Cancelled elections entirely with no future promise
Created fair elections under international monitoring
Created new electoral laws, dissolved the NLD, and established a new pro-military Election Commission — ensuring no meaningful opposition participation
Only delayed elections — keeping the same legal framework
quiz.explanation: The SAC's electoral manipulation went beyond simple postponement: it dissolved the NLD (the party that won 83% of contested seats in 2020), charged Aung San Suu Kyi and other NLD leaders with crimes to disqualify them, created a new Election Commission stacked with military loyalists, wrote new electoral laws requiring party registration under onerous conditions, and charged existing MPs with crimes for their CRPH participation. The result was a planned election without any meaningful opposition participation.

laws.title: Karen National Union and Longest Civil War
laws.subtitle: KNU 75+ Year Struggle
laws.fullDescription: The Karen National Union (KNU) and its armed wing the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) have been fighting for Karen rights and autonomy since 1949 — making it one of the world's longest-running civil conflicts. The Karen — a predominantly Christian ethnic group in southeastern Myanmar — faced displacement and 'Four Cuts' military operations for decades. The KNU signed a preliminary ceasefire in 2012 and participated in peace processes until the coup. Post-coup, the KNU renewed active hostilities, took control of SAC military bases, and allied with the NUG. KNU-controlled areas have hosted many CDM participants and become centers of resistance governance.
laws.penalty: KNU membership in SAC territory: terrorism charges and death penalty; residing in KNU-controlled areas with prior SAC connections: risk when traveling to SAC territory
exceptions: KNU-controlled areas (Kawthoolei — the Karen state the KNU claims) operate under KNU governance law
Karen diaspora in Thailand and Western countries are protected under host country law

quiz.q: Why is the KNU's conflict with Myanmar's government notable historically?
options: It is the most violent conflict in Southeast Asian history
It is the world's longest-running civil conflict — active since 1949 when Burma gained independence
It involved Cold War superpower proxy involvement
It is the only successful ethnic federalism negotiation in Asia
quiz.explanation: The KNU's conflict with Myanmar's government is one of the world's longest-running civil conflicts — beginning in 1949 when Burma was just one year old as an independent nation. The Karen, disillusioned with the new Burman-dominated government's failure to honor wartime promises of autonomy, took up arms for self-determination. The conflict has continued — with periods of ceasefire and negotiation — for over 75 years, spanning multiple generations of fighters, a remarkable longevity by any measure.

laws.title: LGBTQ+ Rights and Criminalization
laws.subtitle: Section 377 and Post-Coup Repression
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Penal Code Section 377 (inherited from British colonial law) criminalizes 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' — used to prosecute gay men, with sentences up to 10 years imprisonment. Under the previous democratic government, there was limited discussion of reform and a small but growing LGBTQ+ civil society. Post-coup, the SAC has expressed more conservative views and LGBTQ+ organizations have been forced underground or abroad. LGBT activists face threats from both security forces and conservative Buddhist nationalist groups. Myanmar Pride events ceased after the coup. LGBTQ+ individuals face particular vulnerability to arbitrary arrest as leverage for other demands.
laws.penalty: Section 377 prosecution: up to 10 years imprisonment; LGBTQ+ organizing: terrorism charges possible post-coup; 'obscene' gender expression: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Private consensual conduct between adults: prosecution requires complaint — not typically proactively policed in urban areas (though this is not reliable protection)
LGBTQ+ Burmese in exile operate freely under host country protections

quiz.q: What is the origin of Myanmar's Section 377 criminalizing same-sex conduct?
options: A post-independence Burmese law reflecting Buddhist values
A 1970s military law
British colonial law — inherited into Myanmar's Penal Code at independence and never repealed
An Islamic law adopted during the colonial period
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's Section 377 of the Penal Code — criminalizing 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' — was originally enacted as part of the Indian Penal Code by British colonial authorities in 1861. It was carried over into Burma's Penal Code at independence in 1948 and has never been repealed. The same provision was the basis for similar laws across former British colonies — though many (India in 2018, Singapore in 2022) have since repealed their versions.

laws.title: Amber Mining and Scientific Ethics
laws.subtitle: Hukawng Valley and Paleontological Controversy
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Hukawng Valley amber deposits have revolutionized paleontology — yielding extraordinary specimens of 99-million-year-old insects, animals, and even feathered dinosaur fragments preserved in three dimensions. However, the amber trade is deeply ethically compromised: mining occurs in conflict-affected Kachin State, KIA taxes the trade, human rights concerns surround extraction conditions, and specimens often lack verified provenance. Scientific journals including Nature have adopted policies against publishing research on amber from Myanmar if post-2017 specimens cannot demonstrate ethical sourcing. The boom in fossil amber prices has driven unprecedented mining intensity, potentially destroying specimens before scientific collection.
laws.penalty: Amber export without SAC permit: criminal prosecution; KIA-taxed amber: technically supports designated terrorist organization under SAC law; selling fossils internationally: subject to export control laws
exceptions: Pre-conflict amber collections with documented provenance can be sold and published without restrictions
Academic institutions sometimes partner with SAC authorities for 'officially sanctioned' collection under controversial arrangements

quiz.q: Why have scientific journals adopted restrictions on publishing Myanmar amber research?
options: Myanmar amber is scientifically inferior to other amber sources
Copyright disputes with Myanmar government over fossil rights
Ethical concerns about amber mined in conflict-affected Kachin State — with human rights issues and KIA conflict financing — making post-2017 specimens ethically compromised
Myanmar amber has been found to contain fraudulent inclusions
quiz.explanation: Major scientific journals including Nature adopted policies restricting publication of research on Myanmar amber because the trade is ethically compromised: mining occurs in conflict-affected Kachin State under conditions involving armed group taxation, potential human rights violations, and conflict financing. The extraordinary scientific value of the specimens creates tension with ethical research standards. Journals now require authors to address provenance and demonstrate specimens were ethically sourced — typically meaning pre-conflict collections or specially documented acquisition.

laws.title: Myanmar's Future Scenarios
laws.subtitle: SAC Collapse, Resistance Victory, or Frozen Conflict
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar analysts identify several plausible futures: (1) SAC military collapse under resistance pressure — accelerating after Operation 1027 and subsequent offensives weakened the military; (2) Prolonged frozen conflict — SAC controls cities/roads, resistance controls rural areas, neither can decisively win; (3) Negotiated settlement — regional powers (China, ASEAN) broker some form of transition; (4) Full resistance victory — unlikely in short term given SAC still controls major cities and military assets. The 'China factor' is decisive: if China withdraws support from the SAC (as it has pressured the SAC on border security and scam compound issues), the junta becomes more vulnerable. The outcome will determine whether Myanmar becomes a federal democracy or a continued military state.
laws.penalty: No legal framework for conflict resolution; post-conflict accountability for atrocities: ICC, ICJ, and universal jurisdiction cases remain open; amnesties: debated between peace and justice advocates
exceptions: Any negotiated settlement would likely include some amnesty provisions — contested between accountability needs and peace requirements
International recognition of a post-SAC government would restore foreign investment and aid flows critical for reconstruction

quiz.q: What role has the 'China factor' played in Myanmar's conflict dynamics?
options: China has fully supported the resistance movement
China has been entirely neutral — refusing all engagement

China's relationship with the SAC is crucial — China supplies military equipment and trade, but has also pressured the SAC on border security issues, making Chinese policy a decisive variable in the conflict's outcome
China has formally recognized Myanmar's NUG as the legitimate government
quiz.explanation: China's relationship with the SAC is arguably the single most important external variable in Myanmar's conflict. China supplies the SAC with military equipment, jet fuel, and trade that enables the junta to survive. However, China has also demonstrated willingness to pressure the SAC — particularly on border security issues (Chinese citizens being trafficked into Myanmar scam compounds) and on the SAC's failure to suppress groups conducting cross-border crime. If China substantially reduces support, the SAC becomes far more vulnerable.

laws.title: Scam Compounds and Cyber Fraud
laws.subtitle: Border Zones and Forced Online Fraud
laws.fullDescription: A humanitarian and criminal crisis has emerged in Myanmar's border areas: criminal organizations — particularly in the Kokang area (MNDAA territory) and Karen State — have built massive compounds where trafficked workers are forced to conduct online fraud. Victims from China, Taiwan, Southeast Asia, and beyond are lured with false job offers, then held against their will and forced to run romance scams, cryptocurrency fraud, and other online crimes targeting victims globally. China has applied significant pressure on Myanmar actors over this issue — since Chinese nationals are among the most trafficked. The KCK Alliance's Operation 1027 was partly motivated by Chinese pressure to address scam compound activities.
laws.penalty: SAC law: human trafficking: criminal prosecution (rarely enforced in border areas outside SAC control); forced online fraud: victims are the ones risking prosecution in their home countries for crimes they were forced to commit; rescuing trafficking victims: requires navigating multiple armed group territories
exceptions: Trafficking victims who escape and reach Chinese territory: China has repatriation programs
UNODC and IOM work on anti-trafficking in border areas under complex access arrangements

quiz.q: What role did Chinese pressure play in Operation 1027?
options: China funded the operation directly
China had no connection to the operation
Chinese pressure on Myanmar authorities to address scam compounds — where Chinese nationals were trafficked — was a significant factor motivating the Brotherhood Alliance offensive
China opposed Operation 1027 as destabilizing
quiz.explanation: China applied significant pressure on Myanmar's SAC and border area armed groups over the massive scam compound operations that were trafficking Chinese nationals in Kokang and other border areas. The KCK Brotherhood Alliance's Operation 1027 — which targeted the Kokang area among others — was partly driven by Chinese demands to dismantle the scam compounds. The operation's success in capturing several major scam compound hubs was seen as fulfilling the Chinese-demanded objective.

laws.title: Chin State Resistance
laws.subtitle: CNF and Mountain Communities
laws.fullDescription: Chin State in northwestern Myanmar — bordering India's Mizoram state — has seen some of the most intense resistance to the SAC. The Chin National Front (CNF) and its armed wing CNA have allied with the NUG. Chinland Defence Force (CDF) groups formed by civilians have fought SAC forces across the mountainous state. The military has responded with severe operations — including aerial bombardment of villages and towns including Mindat. Many Chin civilians have fled to India's Mizoram — which has provided informal refuge despite Indian government requests to return them. Christian Chin communities (Chin people are predominantly Christian — Baptist and other denominations) have strong diaspora connections in Western countries.
laws.penalty: CDF and CNF membership: death penalty under SAC law; Chin civilians crossing to India: Indian immigration law violations; returning to Myanmar from India: risk of SAC arrest
exceptions: Indian state of Mizoram has provided informal refuge to Chin (Chin and Mizo people share ethnic and cultural connections) despite central government concerns
Christian church networks in US, UK, Australia provide advocacy and support for Chin diaspora communities

quiz.q: Why has India's Mizoram state been particularly receptive to Chin refugees despite central government concerns?
options: Mizoram has financial incentives from international donors to host refugees
Mizoram is the closest Indian state and has logistics for refugee management
The Mizo and Chin peoples share ethnic and cultural connections — many Mizo see the Chin as kin, creating social solidarity that overrides central government pressure
Mizoram has abundant land for refugee settlement
quiz.explanation: Mizoram's receptivity to Chin refugees reflects deep ethnic and cultural connections: the Mizo and Chin peoples are closely related — sharing language groups, Christianity (both predominantly Baptist), traditional practices, and in some cases family connections across the porous border. Many Mizo people see the Chin as cousins or kin fleeing persecution, creating social solidarity that has led Mizoram's state government to resist central government pressure to return the refugees to Myanmar.

laws.title: Extrajudicial Killings — Documentation
laws.subtitle: OHCHR Reports and Accountability
laws.fullDescription: OHCHR, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and the Myanmar Witness project have documented thousands of extrajudicial killings — civilians killed in military operations, in custody, and during village attacks. Methods documented: shot while fleeing, burned alive in homes, killed after arrest and before formal detention, executed in groups after capture. High-profile cases include the Kani Township massacre (Sagaing Region, 2021) and multiple events documented with satellite evidence and survivor testimony. The UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar files detailed reports to the Human Rights Council. The IIMM collects evidence systematically. No perpetrators have faced any accountability inside Myanmar.
laws.penalty: International law: extrajudicial killings are war crimes and crimes against humanity — ICC/ICJ/universal jurisdiction potential; SAC domestic law: military operations authorized — effectively no accountability
exceptions: Satellite documentation of specific incidents creates evidentiary basis for eventual accountability
Some perpetrators travel internationally — creating arrest risk in jurisdictions with universal jurisdiction statutes (Belgium, Spain, Germany)
laws.sourceLabel: UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar

quiz.q: What role does the IIMM play in Myanmar accountability efforts?
options: It conducts real-time investigations with authority to arrest perpetrators
It publishes annual reports with no evidentiary collection mandate
It systematically collects and preserves evidence for use in future prosecutions — functioning as a prosecutorial support mechanism
It mediates between the SAC and the NUG
quiz.explanation: The IIMM (UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar) serves as a prosecutorial support body — collecting, consolidating, preserving, and analyzing evidence of serious crimes committed in Myanmar since 2011. Unlike earlier UN human rights reporting bodies, the IIMM is explicitly designed to build case files that can be transmitted to courts with jurisdiction over Myanmar crimes — ICC, ICJ, or universal jurisdiction courts. This prosecutorial orientation makes the IIMM more valuable for long-term accountability than traditional reporting mandates.

laws.title: Plastic Pollution and Coastal Waste
laws.subtitle: Irrawaddy Plastics and Marine Pollution
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar is among Asia's significant contributors to ocean plastic pollution — with the Irrawaddy River carrying plastic waste from inland areas to the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal. Waste management infrastructure is minimal across Myanmar. Urban waste management has further deteriorated post-coup with the governance collapse. Yangon's waste system breakdown has increased plastic waste reaching waterways. Marine debris affects fishing communities and marine ecosystems. Under the SAC, environmental governance including plastic regulation has no meaningful enforcement. International plastic pollution reduction agreements have limited impact in Myanmar given the governance vacuum.
laws.penalty: Under SAC: no meaningful plastic pollution enforcement; industrial waste dumping: rarely prosecuted; international plastic pollution treaties: Myanmar is a signatory but no enforcement capacity
exceptions: UNDP and NGO environmental programs operating in some areas continue waste reduction work
Community-level waste collection programs in urban areas continue with some municipal function

quiz.q: How does Myanmar contribute to ocean plastic pollution?
options: Through direct ocean dumping by fishing fleets
Myanmar has no significant ocean plastic problem
The Irrawaddy River carries plastic waste from inland Myanmar to the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal
Only coastal factories contribute — inland plastic stays inland
quiz.explanation: The Irrawaddy River functions as a conduit for plastic waste from inland Myanmar to the ocean — carrying plastic from urban areas including Yangon and Mandalay downstream through the Irrawaddy Delta to the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal. Studies of ocean plastic pollution have identified major Asian rivers including the Irrawaddy as primary transport pathways. Myanmar's minimal waste management infrastructure means large quantities of plastic enter waterways and eventually reach the ocean.

laws.title: Malaria and Tropical Disease Resurgence
laws.subtitle: Vector Control Collapse in Conflict Areas
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has made significant progress on malaria control since 2010 — with cases declining 70%+ through bed nets, indoor spraying, and rapid diagnostic tests. However, post-coup conflict and healthcare collapse are reversing these gains. In Sagaing, Chin, and Kachin conflict areas, health workers fled (CDM), supply chains broke, and vector control programs stopped. Malaria cases have increased in conflict-affected areas. Drug-resistant malaria in the Greater Mekong Subregion (including Myanmar's Shan border) is a global health concern — resistant parasites could spread to Africa where malaria kills hundreds of thousands annually. Dengue fever outbreaks have also increased with collapsed vector control.
laws.penalty: No Myanmar malaria law penalties; operating health programs in unauthorized areas: risk; SAC checkpoint interference with health supply chains: documented
exceptions: WHO and NGO malaria control programs maintain operations in less conflict-affected areas
Cross-border health cooperation with Thailand on border malaria programs continues under public health diplomacy

quiz.q: Why is drug-resistant malaria in Myanmar a global health concern beyond Myanmar?
options: Myanmar exports malaria-infected mosquitoes
Resistant parasites could spread from the Greater Mekong Subregion to Africa — where malaria kills hundreds of thousands annually
Drug-resistant malaria only affects people with certain genetic profiles
Resistance makes treatment expensive — not more deadly
quiz.explanation: Drug-resistant malaria strains that emerge in the Greater Mekong Subregion (including Myanmar) have historically spread to Africa — where malaria kills hundreds of thousands of people annually, primarily children. When Artemisinin resistance emerged in Southeast Asia, there was major concern it would reach Africa where Artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs) are the primary treatment. Myanmar's conflict-driven malaria control collapse increases the risk that drug-resistant parasites will spread both regionally and globally.

laws.title: Forced Labor and Porterage
laws.subtitle: Military Forced Labor Practices
laws.fullDescription: Forced labor by Myanmar's military has been documented for decades — the ILO (International Labour Organization) has had a special complaints procedure for Myanmar since 1999 (unprecedented in ILO history). The military forces civilians to work as porters carrying military supplies in conflict areas (dangerous — porters are sometimes used as human shields), to construct military facilities, and to provide agricultural labor for military farms. Post-coup, forced labor has continued in conflict areas. The ILO's special Myanmar complaints mechanism allowed forced labor victims to file complaints — a unique international labor accountability mechanism.
laws.penalty: Under international law: forced labor is a serious human rights violation and potential crime against humanity; SAC domestic law: military operations justify requisitioning civilian labor; ILO complaints: diplomatic and trade consequences possible
exceptions: ILO Myanmar Liaison Office maintains some presence and access under its special mandate
Payment of 'compensation' (minimal) for requisitioned labor in some cases creates nominal distinction from pure forced labor

quiz.q: What unprecedented ILO mechanism was established specifically for Myanmar forced labor?
options: A special military exemption from ILO conventions
An ILO emergency fund for forced labor victims
A special complaints procedure (since 1999) — the only country-specific ILO accountability mechanism — allowing forced labor victims to file complaints
A joint Myanmar-ILO compensation fund
quiz.explanation: In 1999, the ILO established a special complaints procedure for Myanmar forced labor — unprecedented in the organization's 80+ year history at the time. The mechanism allowed individuals to file complaints about specific forced labor incidents, creating a unique individual accountability pathway. The ILO took this extraordinary step after documenting systematic military forced labor practices and Myanmar's failure to respond to normal ILO complaints. The mechanism has processed hundreds of cases and created some form of accountability.

laws.title: Youth and Generation Z Resistance
laws.subtitle: Digital Native Protesters and Flash Mobs
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's post-coup resistance has been significantly shaped by Generation Z — young people who grew up with smartphones, social media, and exposure to global culture under the democratic governments of 2011-2021. Gen Z protesters developed creative protest tactics: flash mobs, K-pop inspired performances, artistic demonstrations, and sophisticated social media campaigns. Many have joined the PDF as fighters — rejecting their parents' generation's accommodation with military rule. Youth-led groups (such as the 'Federal Wings') have been particularly prominent. The generation's digital fluency has enabled superior communications and documentation of military abuses compared to previous protest cycles.
laws.penalty: Youth protesters: arrest, torture, imprisonment — younger age provides no legal protection under SAC; joining PDF: death penalty if captured; digital organizing: terrorism charges
exceptions: Youth in exile countries benefit from full legal protection including free speech and assembly
Student unions that relocated abroad continue organizing without Myanmar legal risk

quiz.q: What distinctive characteristic has Myanmar's Generation Z brought to the resistance movement?
options: Military strategy expertise from gaming
Connections to foreign military trainers
Digital fluency — sophisticated social media campaigns, flash mob tactics, and superior documentation of abuses using smartphones
Access to foreign funding through crypto
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's Generation Z protesters — who grew up with smartphones and social media under the 2011-2021 democratic period — brought digital fluency that previous generations lacked. Their creative protest tactics (flash mobs, K-pop inspired demonstrations), sophisticated social media campaigns reaching global audiences, and systematic documentation of military abuses using smartphones transformed how Myanmar's resistance communicated internationally. Their digital capabilities significantly exceeded those of the military, creating information asymmetry favoring the resistance.

laws.title: Banking Sector Paralysis
laws.subtitle: Financial Crisis and Alternative Systems
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's banking sector has been in crisis since the coup. Major banks face: capital flight as depositors withdrew savings, CDM participation by bank employees, SAC seizure of accounts, forced kyat conversion policies, and SWIFT disconnection risk due to sanctions. Many depositors cannot fully access their accounts. Mobile money services (Wave Money, KBZPay) that were growing pre-coup have become critical informal banking alternatives. Chinese Yuan has become a de facto currency in border areas. Hawala networks have expanded dramatically. The SAC created the Myanmar Investment Bank to channel funds but it lacks credibility. Foreign direct investment has essentially stopped.
laws.penalty: Operating unauthorized banking service: criminal prosecution; providing financial services to designated entities: sanctions violation in home country; unauthorized foreign exchange: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Central Bank of Myanmar continues operating under SAC control — maintaining some banking functions
Mobile banking services maintain operations — critical for remittance delivery and commercial transactions

quiz.q: What alternative payment system became critical for Myanmar's economy after the banking crisis?
options: Gold-backed trade only
Barter economy in all areas
Mobile money services like Wave Money and KBZPay became critical for transactions when traditional banking became unreliable
Cryptocurrency replaced banking entirely
quiz.explanation: Mobile money services — particularly Wave Money (a Myanmar-origin mobile wallet) and KBZPay (from KBZ Bank) — became critical financial infrastructure after Myanmar's traditional banking system was destabilized by the coup. These services allowed salary payments, remittances, and commercial transactions when bank branches were inaccessible or when CDM-participating bank staff had left. Mobile money's resilience during the banking crisis demonstrated how digital financial infrastructure can substitute for traditional banking in crisis conditions.

laws.title: Kayah State and Karenni Forces
laws.subtitle: IDP Crisis and Ethnic Resistance
laws.fullDescription: Kayah (Karenni) State has seen some of Myanmar's most intense fighting since the coup — with a high proportion of the population displaced. Karenni Nationalities Defence Force (KNDF) and other groups achieved significant military successes against the SAC. The military responded with airstrikes and village burnings — creating one of Asia's worst displacement crises relative to population. Kayah has the highest proportion of its population displaced of any Myanmar state. The Kayah are predominantly Christian — with Catholic and other church communities providing humanitarian support. The state borders Thailand, and some displacement has reached Thai border areas.
laws.penalty: KNDF membership: death penalty under SAC law; Kayah civilians in SAC territory: interrogation risk regarding resistance connections; crossing to Thailand: Thai immigration enforcement
exceptions: Catholic Church networks provide humanitarian support in conflict areas — with some de facto protection from direct attack
Kayah community organizations in Thai border areas operate under Thai law

quiz.q: What distinguishes Kayah State's displacement crisis from other Myanmar states?
options: It has the largest absolute number of displaced people
It has the highest proportion of its population displaced — a displacement crisis uniquely severe relative to state population
It is the only state where displacement crossed an international border
Displacement in Kayah is entirely temporary and voluntary
quiz.explanation: Kayah State has the highest proportion of its total population displaced of any state in Myanmar — with estimates suggesting over 50% of the state's population has been displaced by conflict at some point since 2021. This extraordinarily high displacement rate reflects both the intensity of the fighting (KNDF and other groups achieved significant military control, prompting severe SAC counter-operations) and the state's small total population (approximately 300,000), meaning even modest displacement numbers represent a large percentage.

laws.title: Dissidents in Exile and Transnational Repression
laws.subtitle: SAC Harassment Beyond Myanmar's Borders
laws.fullDescription: The SAC attempts to silence diaspora opponents through transnational repression — threatening and harassing family members remaining in Myanmar, accessing Myanmar migrant community networks for informants, pressuring non-democratic host governments (including Thailand) to deport critics, and conducting diplomatic pressure campaigns. High-profile exiled journalists, politicians, and activists report surveillance, intimidation, and in some cases physical attacks. The NUG has documented cases of SAC agents operating in Thailand attempting to locate and attack resistance figures. Diaspora Burmese face the agonizing choice between advocacy (risking family members in Myanmar) and silence.
laws.penalty: SAC threats against family in Myanmar: no legal protection for overseas activists' families; SAC agents operating in third countries: host country criminal law applies if caught; deportation of Myanmar dissidents from Thailand: documented
exceptions: Activists in Western countries with strong rule of law have greater protection — SAC cannot pressure these governments to deport them
UN refugee status provides some protection in countries that respect UNHCR determinations

quiz.q: How does the SAC attempt to silence diaspora opponents who are outside Myanmar?
options: By filing international extradition requests
By economic sanctions targeting diaspora Burmese
By threatening family members remaining in Myanmar, using informant networks, and pressuring non-democratic host governments to deport critics
By hacking diaspora activists' social media accounts exclusively
quiz.explanation: The SAC employs transnational repression tactics to silence diaspora opponents: threatening and harassing family members still in Myanmar creates effective pressure on overseas activists to remain silent (the 'family hostage' tactic); informant networks within Myanmar migrant communities in Thailand and Malaysia monitor and report on opposition activity; and diplomatic pressure on non-democratic neighbors (particularly Thailand) has led to deportations of high-profile critics.

laws.title: Tiger Conservation Collapse
laws.subtitle: Hukaung Valley Tiger Reserve
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar was designated a 'tiger range country' with significant populations in the 1990s — particularly in the Hukaung Valley Wildlife Sanctuary (established 2004, expanded 2010 to 21,844 sq km — the world's largest tiger reserve at the time). WCS conducted tiger surveys and anti-poaching programs. However, surveys found tiger populations declining severely — from several hundred to potentially near zero in some areas. Post-coup, WCS and other conservation organizations have withdrawn. Anti-poaching patrols have stopped. The combination of habitat loss (deforestation), snare hunting for wildlife trade, and livestock killing leading to retaliatory poisoning has devastated tiger populations.
laws.penalty: Tiger poaching: criminal prosecution under Wildlife Law (rarely enforced, especially in conflict areas); tiger parts trade: CITES violation; international buyers: prosecuted in their home countries
exceptions: Traditional hunting in communities with ancestral rights in remote forest areas: tolerated though not legally protected
Camera trap monitoring by remote sensing continues without on-ground presence in some areas

quiz.q: What was historically significant about the Hukaung Valley Wildlife Sanctuary?
options: It was Asia's first wildlife sanctuary established by colonists
At its expansion in 2010, it was the world's largest tiger reserve — at 21,844 square kilometers
It was the site of the last confirmed wild tiger birth in mainland Southeast Asia
It was established by the Myanmar military as a conservation showcase
quiz.explanation: The Hukaung Valley Wildlife Sanctuary in Kachin State became the world's largest tiger reserve when expanded in 2010 to 21,844 square kilometers — an area larger than Israel. Despite this impressive designation and WCS conservation programs, tiger surveys found populations declining severely. The gap between legal protection and actual conservation outcomes reflects the persistent challenge of protecting wildlife in areas with weak governance, conflict, and limited economic alternatives to poaching.

laws.title: India's Northeast and Myanmar Refugees
laws.subtitle: Mizoram, Manipur, and Border Communities
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's conflict directly affects India's northeastern states — Mizoram and Manipur share a long border with Myanmar. After the coup, tens of thousands of Myanmar refugees crossed into these Indian states. Mizoram's state government has been broadly sympathetic (ethnic Mizo-Chin kinship). Manipur has been more complex — Kuki-Chin communities in Manipur have their own tensions with the state government, and the Myanmar border has been a conduit for weapons and drugs. India's central government has both humanitarian obligations and security concerns about porous borders enabling arms trafficking and creating instability. India has sought a balance between border security and avoiding full confrontation with Myanmar communities.
laws.penalty: Myanmar refugees in India: Indian immigration law technically requires valid documentation; undocumented entry: deportable; India's central government has pressed for returns despite humanitarian concerns from state governments
exceptions: India's Foreigners Act has some humanitarian provisions that state governments have applied to prevent deportation
Ethnic kinship communities (Mizo-Chin, Kuki-Zomi) receive informal support from corresponding Indian communities

quiz.q: Why has India's Manipur state had a more complex response to Myanmar refugees than Mizoram?
options: Manipur has less land for refugee settlement
Manipur is ruled by a party that opposes all immigration
Kuki-Chin communities in Manipur have their own tensions with the state government, and the Myanmar border has been a conduit for weapons — creating a security dimension absent in Mizoram
Manipur has more economic resources and can support more refugees
quiz.explanation: Manipur's response to Myanmar refugees is complicated by the state's own Kuki-Chin community tensions (Kuki-Chin people have faced violence in Manipur's 2023 ethnic conflict), the cross-border flow of weapons and drugs through the Myanmar border, and the state's more complex political dynamics. Unlike Mizoram — where Mizo-Chin ethnic kinship creates strong community solidarity — Manipur has a more fractious inter-ethnic environment that creates different dynamics around Myanmar border communities.

laws.title: Sesame and Pulse Exports
laws.subtitle: Legal Agricultural Commodities
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar is one of Asia's major producers of sesame and pulses (lentils, chickpeas, black-eyed peas) — primarily exported to China, India, and the Middle East. Before the coup, agricultural exports were a significant foreign exchange earner. Post-coup, agricultural exports have continued to some extent — the SAC needs the revenue. However, conflict in major agricultural areas (Sagaing, Magway), displacement of farmers, banking system disruption affecting agricultural credit, and logistics disruptions have reduced production and export capacity. China continues importing Myanmar agricultural products — one of the SAC's important economic lifelines. Indian importers have also continued purchasing despite the coup.
laws.penalty: Agricultural export without SAC authorization: criminal prosecution; export to sanctioned markets: sanctions violation in buyer's home country; failure to declare agricultural exports to customs: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Subsistence agricultural production and local market sales: not subject to export regulations
Small-scale cross-border agricultural trade in border areas: informally tolerated

quiz.q: Why do Myanmar's agricultural exports continue despite international sanctions?
options: All countries have agricultural sanctions exemptions for food security
Myanmar food exports are not sanctioned by Western countries, and major buyers (China, India) have no sanctions — providing SAC revenue despite political isolation
Agricultural exports have actually stopped completely
SAC has found ways to disguise agricultural exports as humanitarian aid
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's agricultural exports — sesame, pulses, rice — are not targeted by Western sanctions (which focus on military equipment, gems, timber, and individuals), and the major buyers (China and India) have not imposed any sanctions on Myanmar. This means the SAC continues receiving foreign exchange revenue from agricultural exports through channels completely unaffected by Western economic pressure — illustrating how comprehensive sanctions require near-universal participation to be economically decisive.

laws.title: UN General Assembly Recognition
laws.subtitle: Myanmar's UN Seat and Credentials Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Following the coup, Myanmar's UN seat became contested — the SAC claimed Myanmar's UN seat while the NUG's ambassador (Kyaw Moe Tun, appointed pre-coup) refused to vacate. The UN Credentials Committee deferred a decision — effectively allowing the pre-coup ambassador to continue representing Myanmar at the UN. This created an unusual situation: Myanmar's UN seat is formally occupied by someone the SAC considers a criminal. Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun has used Myanmar's UN platform to condemn the coup and advocate for sanctions — remarkable as no UN member state has formally recognized the NUG. The UNGA has passed resolutions condemning the coup and calling for the release of political prisoners.
laws.penalty: SAC's attempted UN representative: currently blocked — Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun holds the seat; Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun: has a SAC arrest warrant — cannot return to Myanmar
exceptions: UN Headquarters (New York) provides diplomatic immunity to the ambassador — SAC cannot arrest him while he operates from UN premises
UNGA resolutions are non-binding — moral authority without enforcement mechanism

quiz.q: What unusual situation exists regarding Myanmar's United Nations representation?
options: Myanmar has been expelled from the UN
The UN has formally recognized the NUG
Myanmar's pre-coup ambassador (appointed by the elected government) continues holding the UN seat — refusing to vacate for the SAC — meaning Myanmar's UN seat opposes the SAC's coup
Myanmar has two separate voting seats — one for the SAC and one for the NUG
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's UN seat is occupied by Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun — appointed by the elected NLD government before the coup — who has refused to vacate for SAC representatives. The UN Credentials Committee deferred the credentials dispute, leaving Kyaw Moe Tun in place. He has used Myanmar's UN platform to condemn the coup, support sanctions, and advocate for democracy — while the SAC has issued an arrest warrant for him and considers him a traitor. The situation has no close parallel in UN history.

laws.title: Forced Conscription Impact
laws.subtitle: Youth Flight and Military Manpower
laws.fullDescription: The SAC's announcement of mandatory military conscription (February 2024) — requiring men 18-35 and women 18-27 to serve — triggered mass exodus. Tens of thousands of young Myanmar citizens fled to Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, and other countries immediately following the announcement. Air tickets from Yangon and Mandalay sold out within hours. The conscription law reflected the SAC's severe manpower shortage — the PDF and EAO offensives have killed large numbers of soldiers, many others have deserted (SAC has documented significant defections to resistance forces), and military morale has plummeted. The conscription announcement further delegitimized the SAC and provided concrete motivation for young people to leave Myanmar.
laws.penalty: Evading conscription: up to 5 years imprisonment under the Military Service Law; assisting conscription evasion: criminal accomplice liability; falsifying medical exemptions: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Students currently enrolled in recognized universities: temporary deferment (vulnerable to withdrawal)
Medical conditions: exemption with certified documentation — subject to military medical board review

quiz.q: What was the immediate public reaction to the SAC's February 2024 conscription announcement?
options: Young people rushed to military recruitment centers
Mass protests in Yangon and Mandalay
Mass exodus — air tickets sold out within hours as tens of thousands fled to Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, and other countries to avoid serving
Quiet compliance — most young people registered as required
quiz.explanation: The SAC's conscription announcement triggered an immediate mass exodus: air tickets from Myanmar's major cities sold out within hours as young people rushed to leave before any enforcement began. The flight demonstrated the depth of public resistance to the SAC — young people were willing to leave their homes, families, and careers rather than serve in a military they viewed as illegitimate and criminal. The exodus further weakened the SAC by depriving it of the human capital it was attempting to conscript.

laws.title: Mekong River Connectivity
laws.subtitle: Myanmar's Eastern Rivers and Regional Hydrology
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Shan State contains the upper reaches of rivers feeding into the Mekong system — critical for Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam. The Salween (Thanlwin) River — one of Asia's last undammed major rivers for significant stretches — runs from Tibet through Shan and Karen states to the Andaman Sea, supporting millions of fisher families. Chinese dam proposals on the upper Salween have been proposed (and resisted by Karen and Shan communities).
