Myanmar's rivers are critical for fish protein, irrigation, and transport across the lower Mekong countries. Post-coup governance collapse has eliminated Myanmar's participation in Mekong regional governance frameworks.
laws.penalty: Under SAC: unauthorized dam construction on navigable rivers: criminal prosecution; illegal sand mining: fines (rarely enforced); overfishing: catch limits not effectively enforced
exceptions: Traditional fishing rights of riverine communities: customary practice recognized in many areas
Emergency fishing for food security during displacement: tolerated

quiz.q: What makes the Salween (Thanlwin) River ecologically significant?
options: It is Asia's most polluted river
It is the longest river originating entirely within Myanmar
One of Asia's last undammed major rivers for significant stretches — supporting rich freshwater biodiversity and fisher communities dependent on seasonal fish migrations
It forms the entire Thailand-Myanmar border
quiz.explanation: The Salween (Thanlwin) River is one of Asia's last remaining major rivers without significant dams for much of its length — allowing unimpeded fish migration from the Andaman Sea into the Shan Plateau highlands. This undammed character supports exceptionally rich freshwater biodiversity and the fisher communities in Karen and Shan states who depend on seasonal fish migrations for protein and income. Proposed dams on the Salween have been strongly opposed by Karen and Shan communities who would be displaced and whose fisheries would be destroyed.

laws.title: Accountability Gap and Impunity
laws.subtitle: No Justice Inside Myanmar
laws.fullDescription: The accountability gap for Myanmar military crimes is profound. No perpetrator of documented atrocities — extrajudicial killings, torture, village burnings, sexual violence — has faced any accountability inside Myanmar. The SAC has dissolved all independent oversight mechanisms. Military courts that nominally have jurisdiction over military misconduct have issued no meaningful convictions for atrocity crimes. International accountability mechanisms (ICC, ICJ, universal jurisdiction) operate extremely slowly and face evidence collection challenges in active conflict. The impunity gap is itself a human rights concern — perpetuating the cycle of violence by demonstrating that atrocities have no consequences.
laws.penalty: International accountability: ICC investigation, ICJ case (Gambia v. Myanmar), universal jurisdiction cases in Argentina (filed 2021) targeting Tatmadaw commanders; SAC domestic: no accountability mechanism
exceptions: Universal jurisdiction cases in Argentina allow survivors to file complaints regardless of location — creating some legal process
IIMM evidence collection is building the evidentiary foundation for future prosecutions — accountability may come decades later
laws.sourceLabel: UN Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar

quiz.q: Where has a universal jurisdiction case targeting Myanmar military commanders been filed outside Myanmar?
options: In Germany — which has universal jurisdiction for genocide
In the United States under the Alien Tort Statute
In Argentina — which has broad universal jurisdiction statutes that have been used for Myanmar Tatmadaw commanders
In the United Kingdom under its International Criminal Court Act
quiz.explanation: A universal jurisdiction case targeting senior Myanmar military commanders was filed in Argentina — using Argentina's broad universal jurisdiction statutes that allow Argentine courts to prosecute international crimes regardless of where they occurred or the nationality of perpetrators or victims. The Argentine 'querella' mechanism was used by survivors and human rights organizations to file complaints against Tatmadaw commanders for crimes against the Rohingya. Argentina has previously used universal jurisdiction for international crimes, making it a receptive jurisdiction for such cases.

laws.title: Buddhist Monk Community Post-Coup
laws.subtitle: Sangha Divisions and Resistance
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Sangha (Buddhist monk community) has been divided since the coup. Many monks have joined protests and resistance — some providing food and shelter to CDM participants and displaced persons. Some monasteries have been turned into PDF training facilities or medical posts. The SAC has arrested monks for anti-coup activity. The State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee (the state-controlled Sangha organization) has largely been compliant with the SAC. Buddhist nationalist monks (associated with 969 Movement and MaBaTha) have had complex relationships with the coup — some supporting military authority, others opposing the coup as exceeding legitimate governance. The traditionally powerful role of monks in political legitimacy has been contested.
laws.penalty: Monks participating in resistance: disrobing (removal of monk status) and arrest; monasteries hosting PDF: targeted for military operations; anti-coup sermons: arrest risk
exceptions: Senior abbots of major pilgrimage sites have some protection due to the religious and cultural significance of attacking them
International Buddhist networks provide some attention to arrested monks — creating advocacy pressure for release

quiz.q: What is the State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee?
options: An anti-coup monk organization
Myanmar's largest Buddhist university
The state-controlled organization overseeing Myanmar's Buddhist Sangha — which has largely been compliant with both previous military governments and the SAC
A meditation center hosting international Buddhist scholars
quiz.explanation: The State Sangha Maha Nayaka Committee (Ma Ha Na) is the state-administered body overseeing Myanmar's Buddhist Sangha — established by the military government in the 1980s to bring the historically independent monk community under state control. The body has powers to discipline and defrock monks, oversee Sangha governance, and mediate between the state and Buddhist institutions. Its generally compliant relationship with military authorities has made it controversial among monks who view it as a compromised institution serving junta interests.

laws.title: Chinese Investment and Belt and Road
laws.subtitle: CMEC and Economic Dependency
laws.fullDescription: The China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) — a component of China's Belt and Road Initiative — envisions infrastructure connecting Yunnan Province through Myanmar to the Indian Ocean. Projects include: Kyaukphyu Special Economic Zone and port (Rakhine State), Mandalay-Kyaukphyu railway, industrial parks, and energy pipelines already operating. China is Myanmar's largest trade partner, investor, and arms supplier. Chinese investment creates dependency — Myanmar needs Chinese economic engagement and political cover (China blocks UNSC resolutions). However, Chinese companies have also faced local resistance (Myitsone Dam), kidnapping risks, and losses from conflict. Chinese investment in conflict-affected areas has declined since 2021.
laws.penalty: Chinese investment projects: subject to bilateral investment agreements — outside normal Myanmar legal framework; Chinese investors in areas of conflict: security risk borne by investors
exceptions: Chinese state-owned enterprise investments have special treaty protections under bilateral investment agreements
Chinese workers in Myanmar have special consular protection arrangements — kidnapping of Chinese nationals triggers strong diplomatic response

quiz.q: What is the significance of the Kyaukphyu port for China's strategic interests?
options: It gives China's navy a base in the Indian Ocean
It would allow Chinese oil imports to bypass the Strait of Malacca by flowing directly from Rakhine to Yunnan via pipeline
It provides China access to Myanmar's fishing grounds
It is a Chinese naval repair facility
quiz.explanation: The Kyaukphyu deep-sea port in Myanmar's Rakhine State is strategically significant because it would allow China to bypass the Strait of Malacca — a naval chokepoint through which most of China's oil imports currently flow. By building pipelines from Kyaukphyu to Yunnan Province, China can import Middle Eastern and African oil directly to its interior without risking naval interdiction at the Strait of Malacca. This 'Malacca Dilemma' strategy is a key driver of Chinese infrastructure investment in Myanmar.

laws.title: Path to Federal Democracy
laws.subtitle: Ethnic Reconciliation and Constitutional Reform
laws.fullDescription: The vision of post-coup Myanmar — articulated by the NUG's Federal Democracy Charter — envisions a genuine federal democracy where ethnic nationalities have territorial autonomy, representation in a federal parliament, control over their natural resources, and rights to their languages and cultures. This would represent a fundamental transformation from Myanmar's 75-year military-unitary state tradition. The unprecedented political alliance between Bamar pro-democracy activists and ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) — forged in the resistance — represents the most promising foundation for such a federal settlement in Myanmar's history. Whether this wartime alliance translates into post-conflict political agreement remains the central question for Myanmar's future.
laws.penalty: Under SAC: advocating for federalism: potential separatism charge; organizing across ethnic lines for resistance: terrorism charges
exceptions: NUG-controlled territories implement federal democracy principles in practice — building constitutional precedents
EAO-NUG cooperation agreements create institutional foundations for post-SAC governance

quiz.q: What is historically unprecedented about the current Myanmar resistance alliance?
options: The use of social media for protest coordination
The involvement of Buddhist monks in resistance

The unprecedented political alliance between Bamar pro-democracy activists and ethnic armed organizations — groups that historically distrusted each other — creating the most promising foundation for federal reconciliation in Myanmar's history
The support of international organizations for the resistance
quiz.explanation: The wartime alliance between the Bamar-led pro-democracy movement (NUG, CRPH, CDM) and ethnic armed organizations represents something historically unprecedented in Myanmar: the dominant Bamar ethnic group and ethnic minorities setting aside decades of mutual distrust to fight a common enemy. Previous pro-democracy movements (1988, 2007) had limited ethnic minority participation. The current alliance — codified in the Federal Democracy Charter — creates the most promising political foundation for a genuine federal settlement if and when the SAC is defeated.

laws.title: Women's Rights Regression Post-Coup
laws.subtitle: Rollback of Progress Under Democratic Governments
laws.fullDescription: Women in Myanmar had made significant progress under the democratic governments (2011-2021) — increasing representation in parliament, entering professional fields, and gaining visibility in public life. Aung San Suu Kyi herself was a global symbol of women's leadership. Since the coup, this progress has been reversed: female civil servants and teachers dismissed following CDM; women face increased sexual violence from the military; restrictions on movement (curfews, checkpoint harassment); and the military's traditionally patriarchal culture dominates governance. However, paradoxically, women have also been among the most prominent and effective resistance leaders — suggesting enduring transformation beneath the surface repression.
laws.penalty: Women participating in resistance: heightened risk of sexual violence in detention; women in CDM: fired and blacklisted; women journalists: arrested and tortured
exceptions: Women in EAO-controlled areas maintain the rights established under EAO governance frameworks — often more progressive than the SAC
NUG cabinet includes women ministers — modeling post-SAC representation

quiz.q: What paradox characterizes women's status in post-coup Myanmar?
options: Women support the SAC more than men
Women face increased repression from the SAC while simultaneously emerging as among the most prominent and effective leaders of the resistance
Women have been uninvolved in both the SAC and the resistance
Women's rights have improved under the coup
quiz.explanation: Post-coup Myanmar presents a paradox: while the SAC's military culture is deeply patriarchal — and women face increased sexual violence, dismissal from professional positions, and general repression — women have simultaneously emerged as among the most prominent resistance leaders. Female protesters sparked the post-coup protest movement; women serve as PDF fighters, underground network leaders, NUG cabinet ministers, and diaspora advocates. The paradox suggests enduring social transformation that the SAC's repression cannot fully reverse.

laws.title: Natural Gas and Pipeline Revenue
laws.subtitle: Shwe Gas Pipeline and Chinese Energy Ties
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has significant offshore and onshore natural gas reserves. The Shwe Gas Project in Rakhine State — a joint venture with Chinese companies — supplies gas via pipeline directly to Yunnan Province. This pipeline generates hundreds of millions of dollars annually — flowing directly to MOGE and ultimately the SAC. The European and American companies that previously operated in Myanmar's energy sector have largely exited post-coup. Chinese and other Asian energy companies continue operating. Energy revenue is the SAC's second-largest revenue source after customs duties. Activist campaigns targeting specific gas revenue flows have had limited success given China's continued purchases.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized natural gas extraction: criminal prosecution; interference with pipeline infrastructure: terrorism charges; energy sector sanctions violations by Western companies: criminal prosecution in home countries
exceptions: Energy sector humanitarian carve-outs allow some fuel imports for aid operations
Pre-existing supply contracts have had authorized wind-down periods

quiz.q: Why is the Shwe Gas Pipeline strategically significant for both Myanmar and China?
options: It supplies Japan — Myanmar's most important trade partner
The pipeline supplies gas from Rakhine directly to Yunnan — providing China with Indian Ocean-adjacent energy without Strait of Malacca transit, while providing the SAC with significant revenue
It is the world's longest undersea pipeline
It connects Myanmar to India's energy market
quiz.explanation: The Shwe Gas Pipeline is strategically significant in both directions: for China, it provides natural gas from Rakhine State directly to landlocked Yunnan Province without Strait of Malacca transit — reducing China's energy vulnerability; for the SAC, the pipeline generates hundreds of millions of dollars annually in gas sales revenue. This mutual dependency creates strong Chinese incentives to maintain working relations with the SAC — making Chinese support for Myanmar sanctions extremely unlikely.

laws.title: Tatmadaw — Military Sociology
laws.subtitle: Structure, Culture, and Motivations
laws.fullDescription: Understanding the Tatmadaw's sociology helps explain its behavior. The military has operated as a 'state within a state' — with its own hospitals, schools, housing, businesses (MEHL and MEC conglomerates), and social ecosystem separate from civilian society. Officers' children attend military schools, receive preferential university admissions, and are expected to follow military careers. This closed social system creates insularity, self-referential culture, and limited exposure to civilian perspectives. The military views itself as the guardian of national unity — seeing ethnic diversity as fragmentation to be managed, and democratic politics as chaos threatening national integrity.
laws.penalty: No legal framework for internal military sociology — relevant to understanding the conflict's structural drivers
exceptions: Former military officers who defected to the resistance (some have joined the NUG or PDF) provide insights into military culture and vulnerabilities
International military-to-military relationships (US, European military attachés) previously sought to influence military culture — all such programs suspended post-coup

quiz.q: What explains the Tatmadaw's insularity and self-referential culture?
options: Military officers are recruited exclusively from Bamar ethnic group
The military operates as a 'state within a state' with its own schools, hospitals, housing, and businesses — creating a closed social ecosystem separate from civilian Myanmar
Military training deliberately removes social empathy
Most officers have studied abroad and lost connection to Myanmar society
quiz.explanation: The Tatmadaw's insularity stems from its comprehensive parallel social system: military children attend Defence Services Schools, live in military housing complexes, receive medical care at military hospitals, and are expected to follow military career paths. This closed ecosystem creates generations of officers who have minimal interaction with civilian society and view the world through the military's institutional lens — including its conception of itself as the indispensable guardian of national unity against ethnic fragmentation and political chaos.

laws.title: Arbitrary Detention Practices
laws.subtitle: SAC Detention Without Legal Basis
laws.fullDescription: The SAC's detention system operates without meaningful legal safeguards. People are detained without arrest warrants, held in unknown locations (enforced disappearance), denied access to lawyers, and subjected to prolonged pre-trial detention. Interrogation torture is routine in initial detention periods. The Penal Code technically requires charging within 24 hours of arrest — but this is routinely violated. Military intelligence holds detainees in undisclosed locations outside any civilian oversight. Some detainees are released after interrogation without charge (having provided information or signed statements); others are charged and face military or civilian courts. AAPP estimates thousands remain in arbitrary detention at any given time.
laws.penalty: Arbitrary detention violates Myanmar law and international law — no accountability mechanism exists; detainees have no effective habeas corpus right; families cannot compel information about detained relatives
exceptions: ICRC requests for prison visits have some success in civilian prisons — though not in military intelligence facilities
High-profile cases with intense international attention sometimes result in release — though this is not a reliable protection
laws.sourceLabel: Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma

quiz.q: What does the AAPP (Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma) do?
options: It provides financial assistance to political prisoners' families exclusively
It is an ASEAN-mandated prisoner monitoring organization
It tracks political arrests, detentions, and killings in Myanmar — providing the most comprehensive accounting of political prisoner numbers and cases
It negotiates prisoner releases with the SAC
quiz.explanation: The AAPP (Assistance Association for Political Prisoners Burma) maintains the most comprehensive database of political arrests, detentions, and killings in Myanmar. Founded by former political prisoners, AAPP tracks each case — including names, charges, detention locations when known, sentences, and deaths in custody. Its data — cited by OHCHR, HRW, governments, and media — provides the evidentiary foundation for understanding the scale of political repression, with total arrest numbers exceeding 20,000 since the 2021 coup.

laws.title: Freshwater Biodiversity
laws.subtitle: Irrawaddy Dolphin and River Ecology
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's rivers — Irrawaddy, Salween, Chindwin — harbor remarkable freshwater biodiversity. The Irrawaddy dolphin (Orcaella brevirostris), a critically endangered freshwater dolphin found in very few river systems globally, inhabits the Irrawaddy. Fishing nets are the primary mortality cause — gillnets entangle and drown dolphins. WCS and local conservation programs previously worked to create dolphin-friendly fishing zones. Post-coup, these programs have been suspended. Freshwater fish biodiversity in the Salween and its tributaries is extraordinary — including species found nowhere else. River pollution from mining, agriculture, and urban waste threatens these unique ecosystems.
laws.penalty: Irrawaddy dolphin killing: criminal prosecution under Wildlife Law; gillnet use in dolphin zones: fines (rarely enforced); river pollution from mining: inconsistent enforcement
exceptions: Traditional fishing communities using traditional methods: customary rights respected
WCS remote monitoring continues using automated acoustic recorders — maintaining some population data without in-country presence

quiz.q: How many river systems globally contain Irrawaddy dolphins in significant numbers?
options: Only the Irrawaddy River in Myanmar
The Irrawaddy, Mekong, and Mahakam rivers — very few systems globally host significant populations
Irrawaddy dolphins are found throughout Southeast Asian coastal waters
More than 20 river systems host Irrawaddy dolphins
quiz.explanation: Irrawaddy dolphins exist in very few river systems globally — the Irrawaddy River in Myanmar, the Mekong (in Cambodia), and the Mahakam River in Borneo host the known freshwater populations. There are also coastal/estuarine populations in Bangladesh and other areas. The Myanmar Irrawaddy population — which gives the species its name — is critically endangered from gillnet bycatch, habitat degradation, and declining river health. Each of these small, isolated populations is irreplaceable.

laws.title: Media in Exile and Information War
laws.subtitle: Free Burma Rangers and Frontline Journalists
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's information environment is characterized by an intense 'information war' between the SAC (controlling state media, RTV, and trying to control telecommunications) and resistance (exile media, citizen journalists, NUG communications). The Irrawaddy, Myanmar Now, DVB, and other outlets operating from Thailand and abroad provide independent reporting. The Free Burma Rangers — a humanitarian relief organization operating in conflict areas since the 1990s — documents military operations and provides medical care in high-risk areas. Citizen journalists with smartphones document village burnings, airstrikes, and killings — uploading to exile media. The information asymmetry favors the resistance: the military cannot fully prevent documentation of its atrocities.
laws.penalty: Citizen journalism: arrest and terrorism charges if caught with documentation; exile media: journalists in Myanmar face death; Free Burma Rangers: face military targeting as 'terrorist supporters'
exceptions: Satellite internet (Starlink has become increasingly available in resistance areas) enables uploads even from remote conflict zones
Encrypted communication platforms allow citizen journalists to transmit evidence with some protection

quiz.q: What role have citizen journalists with smartphones played in Myanmar's conflict?
options: They have been largely ineffective — the military controls all information

Citizen journalists have been the primary source of conflict documentation — uploading footage of village burnings, airstrikes, and killings to exile media, creating an evidence record despite the SAC's information control efforts
Only professional journalists from international media have documented the conflict
Citizen journalism was important early but declined after 2022
quiz.explanation: Citizen journalists — ordinary Myanmar citizens with smartphones — have been the primary source of documentation for Myanmar's military atrocities. Professional journalists cannot operate inside Myanmar without extreme risk, but civilians document village burnings, military operations, and abuses with smartphones and upload to exile media outlets. Organizations like Myanmar Witness and researchers at major universities have analyzed this open-source evidence to document specific incidents and identify perpetrators — creating an evidentiary record for eventual accountability.

laws.title: Rare Earth Minerals
laws.subtitle: Critical Minerals and Chinese Dependency
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar is a significant source of rare earth minerals — used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, electronics, and defense systems. Kachin State produces rare earth elements including heavy rare earths valuable for magnets used in EVs and wind turbines. Myanmar's rare earth exports are overwhelmingly directed to China, which processes virtually all global rare earth minerals. Chinese companies operating in Kachin State (partly under KIA jurisdiction) mine and export rare earths with minimal environmental controls. The strategic importance of rare earths has added a geopolitical dimension to Myanmar's conflicts — making Western countries reluctant to fully decouple from Myanmar's mineral supply chain despite human rights concerns.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized rare earth mining: criminal prosecution (SAC-controlled areas); environmental violations from mining: minimal enforcement; export without permit: customs prosecution
exceptions: KIA-controlled mining areas operate under KIA taxation and governance outside SAC permitting
Emergency mineral supply chain considerations have led some Western countries to maintain pragmatic engagement with Myanmar despite coup

quiz.q: Why are Myanmar's rare earth minerals gaining geopolitical significance?
options: Myanmar has the world's largest rare earth deposits
Rare earth prices have increased 1000% due to Myanmar production

They are used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, and defense systems — creating strategic supply chain dependencies that make Western countries reluctant to fully decouple from Myanmar despite human rights concerns
Myanmar rare earths are uniquely pure — irreplaceable for electronics
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's rare earth minerals have gained geopolitical significance because they feed into global supply chains for critical technologies: electric vehicles (EV motors use rare earth magnets), wind turbines, advanced electronics, and defense systems. China processes virtually all global rare earths, and Myanmar production feeds into Chinese processing. This creates strategic dependencies — Western countries wanting to transition to clean energy and maintain defense capabilities need rare earths, creating tension between human rights concerns and supply chain pragmatism.

laws.title: Mon State and Ceasefire Legacy
laws.subtitle: NMSP and Peace Process Experience
laws.fullDescription: Mon State in southeastern Myanmar offers a case study in peace process limitations. The New Mon State Party (NMSP) and its Mon National Liberation Army (MNLA) had a ceasefire with the Myanmar government since 1995 — one of the longest-standing ethnic ceasefires. During the ceasefire period, Mon areas saw development, some ethnic cultural expression, and economic activity. However, the ceasefire didn't resolve underlying political issues — Mon people continued to lack meaningful autonomy. Post-coup, the ceasefire has been under stress as the NMSP has needed to navigate between SAC pressure and solidarity with the broader resistance. The Mon experience illustrates both the value and limits of ethnic ceasefires without political settlement.
laws.penalty: NMSP membership in SAC territory: SAC and NMSP have complex arrangements — not straightforwardly criminalized but subject to SAC oversight; NMSP members crossing to resistance territory: complex loyalties
exceptions: Ceasefire legacy areas maintain some governance autonomy — Mon cultural expression protected in NMSP areas
Mon diaspora communities in Thailand have long-established advocacy and cultural organizations

quiz.q: What does the Mon State peace experience illustrate about ethnic ceasefires?
options: Ceasefires always lead to comprehensive political settlements
Ethnic ceasefires are always unstable and doomed to fail
Ceasefires provide valuable respite and development opportunities but cannot substitute for political settlement — underlying grievances persist without genuine autonomy and power-sharing
Ceasefires only work when supported by China
quiz.explanation: The NMSP ceasefire experience illustrates that ethnic ceasefires can provide real benefits — reducing violence, allowing development, protecting some cultural expression — but cannot resolve underlying political issues without genuine political settlement. Nearly 30 years of ceasefire didn't give the Mon people meaningful autonomy or democratic representation. The post-coup period exposed the fragility of arrangements built on relationships with a government that changed without reference to the ceasefire structures — demonstrating that ceasefires need political foundations to be durable.

laws.title: Human Trafficking
laws.subtitle: Forced Labor, Sex Trafficking, and Border Exploitation
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar is a major source country for human trafficking — with victims trafficked to China (forced marriage, forced labor), Thailand (fishing industry, sex work, domestic labor), Malaysia, Singapore, and other countries. Post-coup displacement and economic desperation have dramatically increased trafficking vulnerability. Traffickers prey on people fleeing conscription, job seekers in collapsed economy, and displaced communities. The scam compound phenomenon (workers trafficked into border area fraud operations) has attracted global attention. Children are trafficked for domestic labor and sexual exploitation. Under the SAC, anti-trafficking enforcement has declined — and some SAC officials are implicated in trafficking networks.
laws.penalty: Human trafficking prosecution: criminal under Myanmar Penal Code — up to 10 years for trafficking adults, longer for children; but enforcement in SAC-controlled areas targeting officials is minimal; victims trafficked abroad face host country criminal law for crimes they were forced to commit
exceptions: UNODC and IOM anti-trafficking programs maintain limited operations with SAC and EAO authorization
Returned trafficking victims have some support services in urban areas

quiz.q: What economic conditions post-coup have dramatically increased Myanmar trafficking vulnerability?
options: Improved economic conditions have reduced trafficking — people have less reason to seek risky migration
Only conscription evasion has driven trafficking — economic conditions are unchanged
Economic collapse, displacement, conscription flight, and desperate poverty have dramatically increased vulnerability — traffickers prey on people with no legitimate economic alternatives
Only political persecution has increased trafficking
quiz.explanation: The SAC's multiple crises have created unprecedented trafficking vulnerability: economic collapse has eliminated legitimate employment, displacement has created homeless populations without resources, the conscription announcement drove young people to seek any exit from Myanmar, and the banking crisis has made financial desperation widespread. Traffickers exploit each of these vulnerabilities — offering false job opportunities, forced marriage arrangements, and migration pathways that lead victims into trafficking situations.

laws.title: Coral Reefs and Marine Ecosystems
laws.subtitle: Myeik Archipelago and Andaman Sea
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's Myeik (Mergui) Archipelago — over 800 islands in the Andaman Sea — contains some of Southeast Asia's least-disturbed coral reefs and marine ecosystems. The remote archipelago was largely closed to outsiders until the 1990s. Traditional fishing communities — including the Moken ('Sea Nomads') — have lived in harmony with these marine systems for millennia. Since opening to tourism and fishing, the archipelago has faced coral bleaching, dynamite fishing, and overfishing. Marine conservation programs operated in the archipelago pre-coup; most have withdrawn. Post-coup, patrol boats and conservation enforcement have ceased. Illegal fishing by Thai and other foreign boats has increased.
laws.penalty: Illegal fishing in Myanmar waters: criminal prosecution — but enforcement capacity has collapsed post-coup; dynamite fishing: criminal prosecution with minimal enforcement; coral collection: CITES violation
exceptions: Moken traditional fishing rights: customary practice generally recognized — though their communities face multiple pressures
Emergency fishing for food security during conflict displacement: tolerated

quiz.q: Who are the Moken and what is their significance for Myanmar's Myeik Archipelago?
options: A Burmese fishing cooperative
The 'Sea Nomads' — traditional maritime communities who have inhabited the Myeik Archipelago for millennia, living in boats and maintaining ecological relationships with the marine environment
A Mon ethnic subgroup that fishes coastal areas
A Thai fishing community that has settled in Myanmar waters
quiz.explanation: The Moken ('Sea Nomads') are a traditional maritime community who have lived in and around the Myeik Archipelago for millennia — living primarily on boats, moving with seasonal fish migrations, and developing intimate knowledge of the archipelago's marine ecosystems. Their traditional fishing practices are generally sustainable and adapted to the archipelago's ecology. The Moken face multiple pressures: commercialization, sedentarization pressure, loss of fishing grounds to commercial fishing, and exclusion from increasingly developed areas.

laws.title: Regional and Global Response Assessment
laws.subtitle: International Community's Effectiveness
laws.fullDescription: The international community's response to Myanmar's crisis has been criticized as inadequate. Western sanctions have financial impact but are undermined by non-participating major economies. ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus has not been implemented. The UN Security Council is blocked by Chinese and Russian vetoes from stronger action. UNGA resolutions condemning the coup are non-binding. Humanitarian funding is insufficient and access restricted. Arms embargoes are partial — Russia and China continue supplying. The ICC and ICJ processes are slow. Critics argue the international response has been insufficient to change SAC behavior. Defenders argue the constraints are structural — given China's UNSC veto and economic dominance in Myanmar, stronger international action is impossible without Chinese participation.
laws.penalty: No accountability for inadequate international response; structural constraints of UNSC veto power; sovereign equality principle limits intervention options
exceptions: Targeted sanctions can be increased — there remains room for more comprehensive US, EU, UK action
Creative legal strategies (universal jurisdiction, ICJ) provide accountability pathways outside UNSC constraints

quiz.q: What structural factor most limits the UN Security Council's ability to take stronger action on Myanmar?
options: Myanmar is not a UN member state
The UN Charter prohibits intervention in civil wars
Chinese and Russian vetoes block binding UNSC resolutions — meaning the strongest UN accountability measures require Chinese cooperation that China withholds to protect its Myanmar interests
The UN Secretary-General opposes stronger action
quiz.explanation: Chinese and Russian vetoes in the UN Security Council are the primary structural constraint on stronger international action. Both countries have vetoed or threatened to veto binding UNSC resolutions on Myanmar — China to protect its economic interests and client relationship with the SAC, Russia in parallel with its general opposition to Western-sponsored intervention. This veto constraint means that UNSC-mandated sanctions, arms embargoes, or referrals to the ICC require Chinese and Russian agreement — which has not been forthcoming.

laws.title: Tourism Industry Collapse
laws.subtitle: Bagan, Inle Lake, and Post-Coup Visitor Absence
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's tourism industry — which had grown significantly after opening in 2011 to become a significant GDP contributor — collapsed entirely after the coup. Bagan (3,000+ ancient temples), Inle Lake (floating villages and unique leg-rowing fishermen), the royal city of Mandalay, and natural attractions had made Myanmar one of Asia's most compelling destinations. International airlines have stopped or severely reduced service. Foreign governments advise against Myanmar travel. The few tourists who enter are primarily business visitors. Tourism revenue — which supported hundreds of thousands of hotel, restaurant, guide, and transport workers — has essentially disappeared. Post-coup, the tourism infrastructure is maintained by the SAC as a future revenue source.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized tourism operation (unlicensed): fines and closure; tourist facilities in conflict areas: risk of military operations; foreign tourists in restricted areas: arrest risk
exceptions: Government-licensed tourism continues for the few tourists who choose to visit — SAC welcomes the revenue
Some adventure tourism to border areas proceeds informally through Thai operator networks

quiz.q: What made Myanmar's Bagan globally significant as a tourism destination?
options: It contains Asia's largest Buddhist monastery
Over 3,000 ancient temple and pagoda ruins from the Pagan Empire (9th-13th centuries) — one of Asia's greatest archaeological landscapes
It is the site of Myanmar's longest-running festival
It is where Buddhism first arrived in mainland Southeast Asia
quiz.explanation: Bagan in central Myanmar contains over 3,000 ancient Buddhist temples, pagodas, and ruins from the Pagan Empire (9th-13th centuries) — spread across a 104 square kilometer plain. The landscape of ancient spires rising from flat plains at sunrise or sunset is considered one of Asia's most spectacular archaeological vistas, comparable to Angkor Wat. UNESCO designated Bagan a World Heritage Site in 2019. The site attracted hundreds of thousands of visitors annually before the coup destroyed Myanmar's tourism industry.

laws.title: Lack of Rule of Law
laws.subtitle: Judicial Independence Eliminated
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's judicial system has been completely captured by the SAC. Judges are appointed by the junta, their rulings are expected to align with SAC interests, and independent legal practice is severely constrained. Lawyers who represent political prisoners face disbarment, arrest, and imprisonment. Some defense lawyers were charged with crimes for their professional work. The Bar Council is under SAC control. Evidence obtained through torture is used in proceedings. There is no effective habeas corpus. Civilian courts continue handling non-political commercial and family matters — but any case with political dimensions faces predetermined outcomes. The International Bar Association and ABA have documented the judicial system's complete lack of independence.
laws.penalty: Myanmar judges issuing rulings against SAC interests: removal and potential prosecution; lawyers representing political prisoners: disbarment, arrest; legal aid for political prisoners: effectively criminalized
exceptions: Commercial dispute resolution through arbitration (Singapore, Hong Kong venues) provides some independence for contract disputes outside Myanmar courts
Some Myanmar lawyers continue providing informal guidance to political prisoners' families at personal risk

quiz.q: What has happened to lawyers who defended political prisoners under SAC rule?
options: They receive enhanced legal protection as officers of the court
They are allowed to practice freely — attorney-client privilege protects them
Lawyers defending political prisoners have faced disbarment, arrest, and imprisonment — making effective legal representation of political prisoners essentially impossible
Only foreign lawyers face restrictions — Myanmar lawyers have full protection
quiz.explanation: Lawyers who defended political prisoners under SAC rule have faced severe consequences: disbarment (removal of their right to practice law), arrest, and imprisonment on charges including incitement and 'supporting terrorism' for their legal work. Several defense lawyers were themselves arrested and imprisoned after appearing in political cases. This systematic targeting of defense counsel has eliminated meaningful legal representation for political prisoners — the remaining defense lawyers who agree to take political cases operate under extreme self-censorship and fear.

laws.title: Myanmar Humanitarian Crisis Scale
laws.subtitle: 18 Million People Need Aid
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's humanitarian crisis is one of Asia's largest. OCHA's 2024 Humanitarian Response Plan identifies 18 million people in need — nearly 1/3 of Myanmar's population. The crisis encompasses: 2+ million internally displaced, 600,000+ conflict-affected since the coup (in addition to pre-existing crises), food insecurity affecting millions, healthcare collapse, and education disruption. Annual humanitarian funding requirements exceed USD 1 billion — far beyond donor commitments. Humanitarian access is severely restricted in the most affected areas. The SAC imposes administrative restrictions on aid delivery. The scale of need, combined with access restrictions and funding gaps, means millions in acute need receive no assistance.
laws.penalty: Humanitarian workers operating without SAC authorization: arrest risk; aid delivery to resistance-controlled areas: terrorism charges; unauthorized medical care in conflict areas: military targeting
exceptions: UN OCHA coordination mechanism maintains relationships with SAC for humanitarian access — imperfect but essential
ICRC operates under its unique international humanitarian law mandate — though access to conflict areas is constrained

quiz.q: How many people does OCHA estimate are in humanitarian need in Myanmar?
options: About 3 million — primarily conflict-affected
Around 8 million — focusing on food insecurity
18 million people — approximately one-third of Myanmar's total population
Only 500,000 — concentrated in specific conflict zones
quiz.explanation: OCHA's humanitarian assessments identify approximately 18 million people in Myanmar in humanitarian need — nearly one-third of the country's population of approximately 54 million. This extraordinary figure reflects the compounding of multiple crises: conflict displacement, food insecurity from agricultural disruption, healthcare collapse, economic devastation, and pre-existing vulnerabilities. Myanmar's humanitarian crisis rivals in scale some of the world's most recognized emergencies but receives comparatively less international attention.

laws.title: Climate Adaptation Without Governance
laws.subtitle: Heat Stress, Floods, and Agricultural Impacts
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar faces serious climate vulnerabilities — increased heat stress threatening agricultural productivity, more intense monsoon flooding, cyclone intensification, and sea level rise threatening coastal communities. Adaptation to these challenges requires functioning governance: early warning systems, agricultural support, coastal infrastructure, and disaster response capacity. Under the SAC, climate adaptation has essentially ceased — the government neither has the capacity nor prioritizes these concerns. Climate change projections for Myanmar suggest temperature increases that will reduce rice yields, increase heat mortality, and worsen drought and flood cycles. Without adaptation investment, climate change will compound the humanitarian crisis generated by the conflict.
laws.penalty: No Myanmar climate liability framework; climate-displaced communities: no compensation mechanism; agricultural climate adaptation programs: limited to NGO operations in accessible areas
exceptions: UN climate programs (UNDP, FAO) maintain limited adaptation support in less conflict-affected areas
Community-level climate adaptation using traditional knowledge: continues without formal governance support

quiz.q: How does political conflict compound climate vulnerability in Myanmar?
options: Conflict reduces population — decreasing climate vulnerability
Climate and conflict are unrelated — both are independent crises

Conflict destroys the governance capacity needed for climate adaptation — early warning systems, disaster response, agricultural support — leaving climate-vulnerable communities without any protective infrastructure
Military spending competes with climate funding — but governance otherwise functions
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's political conflict compounds climate vulnerability by destroying the governance infrastructure needed for adaptation: early warning systems for floods and cyclones require functioning telecommunications and emergency services; agricultural adaptation requires extension services and credit systems; coastal protection requires engineering and planning capacity; disaster response requires coordinated government machinery. All of these governance functions have been severely degraded by the coup, leaving Myanmar's climate-vulnerable populations without the adaptive capacity they need.

laws.title: Resistance Consolidation and Future
laws.subtitle: PDF Capabilities and SAC Weaknesses
laws.fullDescription: By 2024, Myanmar's resistance has achieved capabilities that few analysts predicted in 2021 — capturing towns, SAC military bases, and border crossings. The PDF has evolved from an untrained civilian force into a more capable fighting organization, often with EAO support and training. SAC military weaknesses include: low morale, significant desertions, heavy casualties from offensives (Operation 1027 and subsequent operations captured over 100 military bases by some estimates), difficulty replacing losses with conscripts, and declining air force capability from fuel restrictions. The resistance faces its own challenges: coordination across diverse forces, post-victory governance planning, and resources. The trajectory as of 2024 is toward SAC territorial erosion.
laws.penalty: No legal framework for this analysis; post-conflict accountability for atrocities: ICC, ICJ, and universal jurisdiction remain open regardless of conflict outcome
exceptions: International humanitarian law principles continue to apply regardless of who gains territorial control
Post-conflict transitional justice processes will require addressing atrocities by all parties — including PDF and EAO abuses as well as SAC crimes

quiz.q: What challenge does the resistance face regarding post-conflict planning?
options: Resistance forces have already agreed on detailed governance plans
The resistance is unified under a single command
Governance planning for a post-SAC Myanmar — coordinating diverse ethnic and political forces with different visions — is a critical challenge that wartime military coordination has not resolved
Only securing sufficient weapons is the resistance's challenge
quiz.explanation: The Myanmar resistance faces a fundamental challenge: wartime military coordination against a common enemy is far easier than post-conflict political coordination over governance. The NUG, CRPH, PDF, and dozens of EAOs have different ethnic constituencies, governance visions, territorial interests, and economic agendas. The Federal Democracy Charter provides a framework but broad political documents don't resolve specific disputes over resource sharing, territory, military command, and governance structures — challenges that will become acute if the SAC falls.

laws.title: Legal Framework After Regime Change
laws.subtitle: Transitional Justice Planning
laws.fullDescription: If Myanmar transitions away from SAC rule, the country faces immense transitional justice challenges: accountability for thousands of documented atrocities, reparations for victims, institutional reform of the military and judiciary, truth and reconciliation processes, and property restitution for those who lost homes and land. Myanmar lacks transitional justice experience — unlike post-apartheid South Africa or post-genocide Rwanda. The tension between accountability (prosecuting perpetrators) and peace (negotiating with military officials who might need amnesty to defect) will be central. International experience suggests hybrid justice mechanisms — combining domestic processes with international support — are most effective for post-conflict accountability.
laws.penalty: No current legal framework; transitional justice laws would be created by a post-SAC government; ICC and ICJ cases continue regardless of Myanmar domestic transitions
exceptions: IIMM evidence collection is preparing for eventual prosecutions — reducing the risk that evidence is lost even if domestic transitional justice is delayed
International community has expressed willingness to support transitional justice mechanisms in a post-SAC Myanmar

quiz.q: What tension lies at the heart of Myanmar transitional justice planning?
options: Tension between military and civilian courts
Tension between Buddhist and Christian approaches to justice
Tension between accountability (prosecuting perpetrators) and peace (potentially needing to offer amnesty to SAC officials who defect to accelerate regime change)
Tension between domestic and international justice mechanisms
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's transitional justice challenge centers on the accountability-peace tension: pursuing full accountability for atrocities may deter SAC officials from defecting or negotiating (fearing prosecution) and could extend the conflict; but offering amnesty betrays victims and leaves unaccountable perpetrators in positions where they could repeat abuses. International transitional justice experience — Colombia, South Africa, Rwanda — shows different societies have made different trade-offs, with hybrid mechanisms often attempting to balance both imperatives.

laws.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Impact
laws.subtitle: Vaccine Rollout Collapse Under Coup
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's COVID-19 response was severely disrupted by the February 2021 coup — just as a vaccine rollout was beginning. CDM participation by healthcare workers left the vaccination program without staff. Healthcare infrastructure collapse meant COVID patients had no treatment access during the Delta wave (mid-2021) — with crematoria overwhelmed and oxygen unavailable in hospitals. Civil society estimates suggest COVID deaths in Myanmar were far higher than official figures indicate — some analyses suggest tens of thousands of excess deaths during the Delta wave. The SAC's COVID-19 statistics are not credible. Vaccine coverage remains among Asia's lowest due to the healthcare collapse.
laws.penalty: No pandemic law enforcement after CDM made public health enforcement impossible; vaccine mandate (briefly attempted): unenforceable
exceptions: UNICEF and WHO maintained some vaccination programs in accessible areas — though severely limited
Informal vaccine delivery through underground healthcare networks operated by CDM-affiliated health workers

quiz.q: How did the 2021 coup affect Myanmar's COVID-19 response?
options: The coup had minimal impact — health workers continued regardless
The coup improved COVID response by ending corrupt procurement

The coup devastated the response: CDM by healthcare workers gutted the vaccination program, healthcare infrastructure collapse left COVID patients without treatment during the Delta wave, causing tens of thousands of estimated excess deaths
The coup delayed vaccine delivery by only a few weeks
quiz.explanation: The February 2021 coup devastated Myanmar's COVID-19 response: CDM (Civil Disobedience Movement) participation by thousands of nurses, doctors, and health workers essentially shut down the vaccination program that had just begun; hospital closures during CDM meant COVID patients had nowhere to go during the Delta wave (mid-2021); oxygen shortages caused deaths that adequate hospital care would have prevented. Civil society analysts estimated Myanmar's actual COVID death toll during the Delta wave far exceeded official figures — potentially representing tens of thousands of preventable deaths directly caused by the coup's destruction of healthcare capacity.

laws.title: Agricultural Biodiversity Loss
laws.subtitle: Heritage Rice and Traditional Varieties
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar has extraordinary agricultural biodiversity — particularly in rice varieties. The country maintained thousands of traditional rice varieties adapted to specific local conditions (flood-resistant, drought-resistant, aromatic, medicinal) developed over millennia by farming communities. The International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) has noted Myanmar as one of Asia's most important centers of rice genetic diversity. High-yielding modern varieties have been replacing traditional ones since the 1970s green revolution. Post-coup agricultural disruption — land abandonment, displacement of farming communities, loss of seed saving practices — threatens traditional variety preservation. Once lost, this genetic diversity cannot be recovered.
laws.penalty: No Myanmar agricultural biodiversity law; traditional variety loss: no formal prohibition; seed saving: customary practice without formal legal protection
exceptions: IRRI and international seed banks maintain ex-situ collections of Myanmar rice varieties — preserving genetic material outside the country
Some farming communities continue traditional seed saving as cultural practice despite displacement

quiz.q: Why is Myanmar's rice genetic diversity globally important?
options: Myanmar produces the most rice globally
Myanmar rice is uniquely nutritious

Myanmar maintains thousands of traditional varieties representing millennia of adaptation to diverse local conditions — a gene bank of irreplaceable agricultural biodiversity that could be critical for future food security under climate change
Myanmar rice varieties are prized for cooking quality in international markets
quiz.explanation: Myanmar's thousands of traditional rice varieties represent millennia of farmer selection for local adaptation — flood resistance, drought tolerance, pest resistance, medicinal properties, and culinary qualities suited to specific microclimates. This genetic diversity is the raw material for future crop improvement under climate change — when varieties adapted to new temperature and rainfall patterns will be needed. The loss of these traditional varieties through agricultural disruption would be irreversible — eliminating genetic options that humanity may critically need in coming decades.

laws.title: Myanmar's International Legal Status
laws.subtitle: Non-Recognition and State Continuity
laws.fullDescription: Myanmar's international legal status is unusual: the SAC controls most major cities and national infrastructure, but no democratic country formally recognizes the SAC as Myanmar's legitimate government; simultaneously, the NUG is not recognized as the government despite having been elected. Myanmar's UN seat is held by a pre-coup ambassador who opposes the SAC. Myanmar remains bound by all pre-coup treaty obligations under state continuity doctrine. This 'recognition gap' — where neither the de facto power nor the democratically legitimate government has full international recognition — creates a gray zone in international law. Myanmar's trajectory may determine how international law develops around recognition of coup governments in democratic backsliding states.
laws.penalty: SAC officials face potential prosecution in countries with universal jurisdiction despite non-recognition of the SAC; Myanmar state obligations continue regardless of government change
exceptions: Humanitarian law obligations apply to all parties controlling territory — regardless of recognition status
UN system pragmatically engages the SAC on humanitarian matters while withholding political recognition

quiz.q: What international law principle means Myanmar remains bound by pre-coup treaties despite the government change?
options: Treaty succession
Customary international law override
State continuity — the state of Myanmar continues to exist and bear treaty obligations regardless of which government controls it
Force majeure — coup events nullify prior commitments
quiz.explanation: State continuity is the international law principle that a state remains the same legal entity — and bound by the same international obligations — regardless of changes in government, even dramatic ones like coups. When the SAC seized power, Myanmar as a state continued to be bound by all treaties, UN Charter commitments, Geneva Conventions, and other international obligations made by previous governments. This means Myanmar cannot escape accountability for violations of these obligations by claiming a new government with no connection to prior commitments.
